The other covers how the north called up its own young men. The pairing shows the war's manpower and prisoner questions side by side.
cia-0000015330: A letter to Coral Lorenson from John Warner fills a CIA file dated November 2, 1960. Warner refers her letter on to the Air Force, per the title. Most saucer mail that reached the agency was sent on just this way. The file holds the polite hand off given to one more citizen writer.
cia-0000015430: Declassifying a CIA report on UFOs was requested by the Air Force in a record dated July 2, 1966. The two services had shared the saucer problem for years, with the Air Force in the public lead. Opening an agency report would expose how the CIA had judged the same reports. The file keeps the request itself, a small marker of a wider push for openness.
cia-0000020430: Chile's government meant to step up its diplomatic, commercial, and propaganda work abroad, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. The clipped title lists three fields of effort in a row. Salvador Allende's government was then seeking friends and trade under growing strain. Reading a rival government's plans to sell itself abroad was standard work for the agency's Chile watchers.
cia-0000022330: A Soviet article claimed the United States buys spies, and the CIA kept it in a record dated in 1960. The piece belonged to the press war around the Powers trial that year. Moscow used the case to paint American intelligence as a market in hired men. Filing enemy articles let analysts track the lines being sold to Soviet readers at home.
cia-0000028530: Two American pilots held captive in Laos were transferred to North Vietnam, a CIA record dated in 1968 reports. A transfer moved the men farther from any rescue and into the main prison system. Such moves were tracked closely, since a man's place shaped every plan for him. The entry adds one hard journey to the long record of the Laos missing.
cia-0000044430:
Havana blamed the Salvadoran army for the priest killings, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. Cuba supported the rebels in El Salvador's civil war. Its charge against the army came as no surprise to any reader.

Inside, the Cuban accusation is preserved as Havana delivered it. Expected or not, the charge added a foreign voice to the chorus. It also served Cuba's own contest with the United States by proxy. The file shows the murders entering the region's wider argument, in which each capital used the crime to score points against its enemies abroad.
cia-0000045930: An official arrived for talks about Americans missing in Vietnam, and a CIA item dated June 5, 1991, noted the visit. Such trips were the working machinery of the accounting effort, meeting by meeting and list by list. The brief report marks one stop in a process that ground on for years after the war.
cia-0000049130: Findings of the Special Honor Commission in the San Sebastian case fill a CIA item from 1989. An honor commission was the armed forces' own court of inquiry, judging soldiers by the institution's code. Its findings carried weight inside the army even when outsiders doubted them, and the file kept them for the record.
cia-0000049230: A 1992 letter from the CIA's deputy director for operations to Congressman Bud Shuster survives in this item. The letter relates to a Salvadoran general whose name the title cuts off after Juan. Shuster had pressed the Jesuit case hard in Congress, and letters like this one were the agency's formal answers.

Ken Kron and colleagues discovered novel hypermethylated genes in prostate cancer using genomic CpG island microarrays, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Promoter methylation regulation of tumor suppressor genes is a common feature of many cancers. Such silencing may contribute to cancer development, including prostate cancer. Prompting genome wide searches for newly methylated loci that could serve as biomarkers or reveal pathways.

Microarrays scanned CpG islands for abnormal methylation gains. Novel candidates emerged for validation as markers. Methylation tests could aid early detection. Some genes may also be therapeutic targets. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0005430:
Rebekah Bartelt and colleagues compared two kinds of T cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. T cells help clear germs from the body, but when they switch on at the wrong time they can cause disease. Labs often study long-lived T cell lines grown in dishes instead of fresh cells from blood.

The team set off the T cell receptor in both kinds of cells and compared the signals that followed. They also compared what the cells did next, such as making signals and dividing. Any gaps between the two warn workers not to trust cell lines too far when studying real immune responses.
plos-pone-0005530:
Jing Du and co-authors studied chemicals released by brain cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Chemicals made by nerve cells affect how nearby cells work and stay healthy. Whether those chemicals play a role in Alzheimer's disease was unknown.

The team compared chemicals from two brain cell types: cells of the cerebellum and cells of the hippocampus. The two sets had opposite effects linked to the disease process. That contrast hints that where a chemical is made in the brain may decide whether it helps or harms in Alzheimer's disease. The result warns against treating all brain regions as one in studies of this disease.
plos-pone-0005630:
Claudio Marinho and co-authors studied malaria in pregnant mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Malaria in pregnancy harms the placenta and leads to poor outcomes for mother and baby. The ways the parasite expands during pregnancy are hard to study in people.

Using new mouse tools, the team tracked parasites that returned after a first infection in pregnancy. Those parasites bound more strongly to the placenta. Mothers who had been through it once gained protection in later pregnancies, a pattern the model can now be used to explain. Malaria in pregnancy is a leading cause of low birth weight in the tropics, so models of it carry weight.
plos-pone-0005730:
Yervand Karapetyan and colleagues sped up the typing of prion strains in 2009. Prions are misshapen proteins that cause fatal brain diseases, and each strain behaves in its own way. Old typing methods took months of watching disease in mice, plus detailed brain checks.

The new method grows prions fast in special mice, then reads the strain with a panel of test cells. Faster typing matters when a new case appears in cattle, deer, or people. It can show quickly whether the strain matches a known threat. The team details how the shortcut holds up against the slow standard.
plos-pone-0005830:
Tammy Westmoreland and co-authors screened yeast in 2009 for genes that protect against the chemo drug doxorubicin. The drug breaks DNA double strands, which kills cancer cells but also harms healthy ones. Finding resistance genes in yeast can reveal the same defenses in human tumors.

The team tested a full set of yeast strains, each missing one gene, in its diploid form. Hundreds of strains proved sensitive to the drug, outlining a conserved repair network. Because the network is shared with humans, its members are leads for making tumors more drug-sensitive. Yeast again serves as a fast first draft.
plos-pone-0006430:
Miaozong Wu and co-authors studied aging muscle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper centered on a protein called Akt. Old skeletal muscle shows more metabolic and functional problems. Left unchecked, these problems raise illness and death rates. The team looked at why Akt, also called protein kinase B, works less well as muscle ages.

They linked the decline to a chemical change called S-nitrosylation. They also tested acetaminophen, a common pain drug, as a way to intervene. The study connects a basic cell signal to the weakness of old muscle. It hints that a familiar drug might help protect aging muscle function.
plos-pone-0006530:
Paige Davies, Anne Powell, John Swain, and colleagues studied cell fusion in the intestine for PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell fusion between circulating bone marrow-derived cells and other cells is well documented in various tissues. It has recently been suggested to occur in the intestine as well. The team examined how inflammation and proliferation act in this process.

Their title reports that inflammation and proliferation act together to mediate intestinal cell fusion. Two signals together may create the conditions fusion needs. Fusion could contribute to gut repair, or to disease when misdirected. The study clarifies when bone marrow cells merge into gut tissue.
plos-pone-0006630:
Kheng Chheng and co-authors reported drug-proof staph infections in Cambodian children in PLOS ONE in 2009. In rich lands, community-linked MRSA, a form of Staphylococcus aureus that resists key drugs, is on the rise. It has seemed rare in poor lands, but data there are thin. The team studied the rise of this form in infections of children in Cambodia.

Finding this form on the rise there changes how doctors should treat staph cases. First-choice drugs must now cover the drug-proof strain. Watch systems in less studied places often find such problems late. Their report is an early warning for the whole region.
plos-pone-0009430:
Martine Humbert and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on a hard to treat cancer of the pancreas. Some growth signals run too high in these tumors. One drug, masitinib, blocks several of those signals. The team paired it with gemcitabine, a drug long used for this cancer.

The pair was tested on human tumor cells grown in the lab. It was also tested in mice that carried human tumor tissue. The authors report how the two drugs acted together in both settings. Their work tests whether a paired approach could do more than a single drug alone.
plos-pone-0009530:
Annette O'Connor and colleagues reviewed health studies near large animal farms in PLOS ONE in 2010. Animal feeding operations house many livestock in a small area. People who live nearby often report health complaints. The review gathered studies on breathing, gut, and mental health in such neighbors. It weighed how strong and consistent the evidence is.

Pulling the studies together shows where links are firm and where they are weak. Many reports rely on what people say about their own health, which can bias results. The authors set out what better studies would need. Their map helps officials judge real risks around these farms.
plos-pone-0009630:
Theresa Manful and co-authors hunted for a better test for sleeping sickness in PLOS ONE in 2010. The East African form is caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense. Diagnosis still rests on finding the parasite in blood under a microscope. That method misses cases and needs skilled staff. The team screened the parasite's proteins for ones that patients' antibodies recognize strongly.

Proteins picked out by patient blood are candidates for a simple antibody test. The team also cloned the genes for the most promising ones. A field friendly test would speed treatment of a disease that is fatal if missed. The study supplies the raw material such a test needs.
plos-pone-0010430:
Patrycja Dubielecka and colleagues studied how cells gulp fluid, and how two protein versions steer that gulping, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gulping process, macropinocytosis, lets cells take in fluid and large molecules. It depends on the cell's inner skeleton reshaping near the surface. A protein called Rac1 was thought to trigger that reshaping through a partner complex. The authors focused on two forms of a related protein, Abi1.

The two forms regulated the gulping process differently. Small differences in one protein can thus tune a whole cell behavior. Cells use gulping to feed, to sample their surroundings, and sometimes to let viruses in. Cancer cells also exploit it to fuel growth. Sorting the regulators may reveal ways to block those abuses.
plos-pone-0010530:
Anna Liisa Suominen-Taipale and colleagues checked whether eating fish tracks with fewer depressive episodes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fish and their omega-3 fats are often said to protect mental well-being. The evidence behind that claim, though, was conflicting. The team ran a cross-sectional analysis in a Finnish population sample. They compared fish intake, omega-3 intake, and blood levels of these fats against depression history.

Looking at diet and blood measures together strengthens the check. Blood levels show what the body actually absorbed, not just what people report eating. Cross-sectional data cannot prove cause, and the authors treat it accordingly. Still, large population analyses help settle whether the fish-mood link deserves trials. Mental health nutrition needs exactly this kind of careful accounting.
plos-pone-0010630:
Jin-Hyeok Hwang and colleagues searched for a marker that predicts chemotherapy success in pancreatic cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Surgery can remove the tumor, yet the cancer often returns. Added drug treatment helps some patients and only burdens others.

The team measured a tiny molecule, microRNA-21, in tumor samples. Patients with high levels fared worse and gained less from added treatment. Low levels marked a group that benefited more. A simple tumor test of this kind could spare some patients harsh drugs that would not help them, and focus care where it works.
plos-pone-0010730:
Jatin Shah and colleagues gathered studies on why people in India join clinical trials, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trials have globalized fast, with many now run in India. That growth raised fair questions about consent, trust, and whether local customs are respected during recruitment.

The meta-analysis combined findings from many interview-based studies. Hope for better care, trust in doctors, and family advice recurred as motives. Payment mattered less than outsiders often assume. Knowing real motives helps ethics boards write rules that protect volunteers without blocking research that local communities actually welcome.
plos-pone-0010830:
Yair Fisher, Anna Nemirovsky, Rona Baron and colleagues reported this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer's disease fills the brain with clumps of a protein fragment called amyloid-beta. The team tested whether vaccinating mice against that fragment would draw immune T cells to the plaques and help clear them away.

Vaccination with amyloid-beta sent T cells to gather at plaques in the brain, and the plaques were almost fully cleared. A comparison vaccine using a spinal cord protein sent its T cells to the spinal cord and caused harmful inflammation there instead. The amyloid-targeted cells also raised markers linked to cleanup activity in the brain. Fisher and colleagues offer early evidence that a carefully aimed immune response might remove plaques without attacking healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0010930:
Por Ir, Chean Men, Henry Lucas and co-authors published this health survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. Serious illness is a known route into poverty in developing countries, through treatment bills and lost work, but measuring that impact well is difficult. As part of an international project, the team surveyed rural Cambodia to find households hit by major illness.

Nearly six thousand households across three rural health districts were interviewed after random cluster sampling. In more than a quarter of them, at least one person had suffered a serious illness during the recall period. Those households were flagged for deeper interviews about costs, coping, and livelihood damage. Ir and colleagues supply the screening half of a poverty-and-illness study, showing how common the shock of major sickness is in the Cambodian countryside.
plos-pone-0011030:
Lee Yee Choong, Simin Lim, Poh Kuan Chong and co-authors published this breast cancer proteomics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tracking how breast cancer develops is hampered by the genetic and environmental noise between patients. The MCF10AT model avoids that noise: four cell lines descended from the same source, each mimicking a later stage of progression, grown as grafts.

Using isotope-tagged mass spectrometry, the team measured more than twelve hundred proteins across the model. Nearly a hundred proteins changed significantly between stages, spanning twenty functional groups including kinases, proteases, adhesion, and skeleton proteins, and the number of changed proteins grew as disease advanced. Choong and colleagues supply a stage-by-stage protein map of breast cancer progression, a cleaner hunting ground for markers and drug targets than patient samples alone.
plos-pone-0011130:
Madronal, Lopez-Aracil, Rangel and colleagues raised mice in varied settings for PLOS ONE in 2010. Some mice lived in rich spaces with more room to move, objects to explore and cage mates to meet. The team then tested movement, learning and new brain cell growth.

Mice from rich settings performed better and grew more new cells in a brain region tied to memory. The gains show how daily surroundings shape the brain in lasting ways. That supports the value of active, social settings for brain health. It also gives lab studies a warning: plain cages may understate what a brain can do.
plos-pone-0011230:
Pond, Delport, Muse and colleagues corrected a gene analysis bias in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models of how the genetic code evolves need starting estimates for how often each code word appears. Common shortcuts guess those rates instead of measuring them, and the guesses can bias results.

The team showed how to correct that bias in empirical estimators used by the models. Sharper estimates improve family trees built from gene data. Better trees give better dates for when genes and species split. The fix is a small change with wide use, since codon models are a daily tool in evolution research.
plos-pone-0011330:
Tamar Dvash, Neta Lavon, and Guoping Fan studied female human stem cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Female cells carry two X chromosomes, and early in growth one X is normally shut down so gene doses stay balanced. The team used stem cells taken from early embryos to watch when and how that shutdown begins.

They found that cells in their earliest passages do not all shut down the X in the same way. Some had started the process, others had not, and the pattern shifted as cells were grown longer. That uneven start matters for anyone using these cells in research. A lab that assumes all female stem cells behave alike may misread its results, so the paper urges care in checking each cell line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1230:
A second Togo cable to Sato is dated 21 July 1945. Two instructions in a day show Tokyo leaning hard on its Moscow channel. The summit in Germany was moving toward a public word on Japan, and Tokyo sensed its time shrinking.

Togo's messages balanced two needs: keep the Soviet door open, and keep Tokyo's own hard-liners from shutting the whole bid down. That balance runs through his words to Sato. This cable is one piece of it. Preserved through American codebreaking, it lets readers watch a beaten empire's last diplomacy from inside its own wires.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1330:
Britain's team tabled this proposal on 21 July 1945. It came from the end of the summit's first week, while Churchill still led the British side. The paper set London's stand on its point for the other teams to answer.

British papers of the first week carry a poignancy their writers could not feel. The government behind them was about to fall, and new men would own the stands taken here. This proposal is part of that first-week British hand. It survives in the American record, where readers can set it against the final terms and judge what the change of leaders cost or saved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1430:
A second Soviet text dated 29 July 1945 follows in the closing run of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

The Soviet habit of tabling full drafts forced the other sides to argue on Moscow's paper or spend time writing their own. This text is part of that pressure, applied as the talks neared their end. For readers, the run of Soviet drafts is a study in negotiation by document: claims fixed in ink, defended clause by clause. What survived into the protocol can be checked line by line from these pages.
frus-1945-50-intel-d30:
General Clayton Bissell, the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, wrote to Secretary of War Patterson on 22 October 1945. Bissell spoke for the Army's own intelligence arm, G-2. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The Army's intelligence chief had his own claims in the postwar settlement, separate from the SSU remnant housed in his department. His memorandum to the secretary shows G-2 stating its case at the top. Readers should keep the Army's threads distinct: Magruder's leftover OSS men and Bissell's uniformed service were rivals inside one building. The volume prints both sides, and the friction between them shaped what the Army finally asked for.
frus-1945-50-intel-d130:
Strategic Services Unit General Orders No. 16, dated 19 October 1946, is among the SSU's last papers in the volume. General orders announce a unit's internal acts: postings, honors, and endings. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By October 1946 the SSU's secret operations had largely passed to the Central Intelligence Group, and the remnant was winding down. A numbered order from that season has the flavor of a colors ceremony in prose. Readers who followed the unit from Magruder's first letters will feel the thread close. The OSS's last ember was kept alive for a year by careful paper. Here it dims toward its end, as its work lives on in a new house.
frus-1945-50-intel-d230:
A memorandum from the Secretary of the Army (Royall) reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 26 November 1947. Readers meet it as document 230 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d330:
On 18 November 1947, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). It survives in print as document 330 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d430:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 11, dated 6 January 1950, is document 430 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The directive opened the rule making of a new decade. By 1950 the CIA had rivals, partners, and a record of its own to defend. A fresh standing order at that point shows the Council still tuning the balance among them, three years after the agency began. The 1950 directives speak to a system that now had to manage success and strain alike. A new decade found the rule book still open, still being written by use.
frus-1861-d30:
Henry Sanford sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 July 1861. It is document 30 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford wrote three days before the battle of Bull Run was fought in Virginia. His letter crossed the ocean in a world that did not yet know the result. That gap between event and report is the true pace of diplomacy in 1861, and this letter marks it plainly. The steamship mails set the pace of his work, each packet bringing a fresh batch of tasks. Each packet from home reset his tasks, and he worked through them in order.
frus-1861-d130:
On 12 June 1861, William Dayton reported the new French stance to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 130 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton reported a Paris that had now stated its neutral course. The task shifted from shaping the stance to policing it. His mid June letter marks that turn, from the drama of decision to the grind of watching its use. Policing a neutral stance meant protests, claims, and proof, week after week. Proof, in such work, was a matter of ship names, dates, and sworn words. The turn he marks governed the file from then on.
frus-1861-d230:
In a letter dated 14 September 1861, William H. Seward gave Mr. Fogg his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 230 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d30:
In a letter dated 10 March 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 30 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d130:
Seward wrote again on 18 August 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 130 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d230:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 September 1862, in a letter printed as Document 230 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Stuart letters under that date.

Stuart wrote in the immediate wake of Bull Run, with Lee's army about to cross into Maryland. British policy turned on whether the South could prove itself a lasting nation in the field. A legation letter from this week reached London as ministers there weighed that proof. Its place in the file marks how closely diplomacy tracked the armies. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d330:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, resumed the Paris mail on 3 October 1862 with a dispatch to William L. Dayton, printed as Document 330 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Seward letters to Dayton under that date in the wider file.

Early October found France ready to propose a truce jointly with Britain and Russia, waiting only for London's word. Seward's letters to Paris in this window carried the Union's refusal in advance: no foreign plan for the war would be accepted. This dispatch belongs to that firm autumn line. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d430:
On 28 June 1862 Gabriel García Tassara, Spain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is Document 430 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Tassara had served in Washington for years and knew American politics well, which made his notes a fair test of Spanish feeling. In the summer of 1862 Spain was pulling out of the joint Mexican venture while France pressed on alone. The questions between Madrid and Washington ran from that expedition to Confederate activity near Cuba. A note like this one kept those matters in formal channels, where Seward preferred to handle them.
frus-1862-d530:
A second note of 7 June 1862 went from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 530 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Same-day pairs were common when a minister transmitted separate enclosures or took up two questions that protocol kept apart. The Dutch business of that week in Washington ran alongside the Hague correspondence of Minister Pike, and the two files illuminate each other. Van Limburg wrote as the resident voice of a small maritime power dealing with a great republic at war. His notes, formal and exact, are the Washington half of one of the volume's most complete small-country records.
frus-1862-d630:
Edward Joy Morris wrote from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 March 1862. His report is Document 630 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Spring 1862 found Morris reporting the Levant's quiet: American commerce moving, citizens protected, the war a subject of curiosity rather than policy at the Porte. Such reports had a negative value Washington appreciated, the assurance that one whole region required nothing. They also carried the minister's observations on the Eastern Question. That was the standing rivalry over Ottoman lands. American merchants felt it in every port from Smyrna to Beirut. The letter sustains the Turkish file's calm, expert tone.
frus-1863p1-d30:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 30 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-January letters from Adams weighed how Britain was taking the new year of the war. The freedom edict had stirred the British public, and the legation tracked that stir with care. Adams's cool style suited the work: he reported what he saw, not what he hoped. This dispatch is a fair sample of his craft, and of the file that made his name as the Union's man in London.
frus-1863p1-d130:
London's late-March mail includes this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 26 March 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 130 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-March mail from London came as the ship fight neared its peak. Adams reported talks, press, and the state of the yards for Washington's use. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. In the run of the volume it stands in one of the thickest weeks of the file. Both capitals wrote hard on the same points that week.
frus-1863p1-d230:
Reporting on 9 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 230 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d330:
Writing in Washington on 29 November 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 330 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d430:
A 28 March 1863 dispatch from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d530:
A dispatch dated 23 May 1863 went from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d630:
From William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 14 October 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020030:
Simon K. Cheng, Felix Olale, Ali H. Brivanlou, and their group untangled a signaling path in PLOS Biology in 2004. TGFβ signals guide how embryos grow. A protein family called EGF-CFC helps some of those signals reach their targets, and a blocker called Lefty can shut them down.

The team shows that Lefty works by jamming the EGF-CFC helpers. It stops some TGFβ signals, such as Nodal, while leaving others alone. That fine control matters in the early embryo, where signal strength sets body axes. The work explains one way embryos keep strong growth signals on a short leash, and why losing that leash can distort development.
plos-pbio-0020130:
Patrick Seale, Jeff Ishibashi, Anthony Scimè, and co-workers tested stem cells from hurt muscle in PLOS Biology in 2004. A marker protein called Pax7 is the sign of muscle stem cells. The team worked with a blood-linked stem cell group found in injured muscle and asked what Pax7 does there.

Adding Pax7 was enough to steer those cells toward becoming muscle, and without it they could not take that path. So Pax7 is both needed and sufficient for the switch, a strong claim in stem cell work. The result points to a master control for muscle fate. If that control can be used safely, it might one day help repair muscle lost to injury or disease.
plos-pbio-0020230:
Margaret J. Mackinnon and Andrew F. Read modeled a hard trade-off in malaria in PLOS Biology in 2004. Malaria parasites grow inside red blood cells, and the immune system fights them. The authors ask how that fight shapes the evolution of the parasite's virulence, meaning how sick it makes the host.

Their model suggests strong immunity can favor tougher, faster-growing parasites, since only those thrive under attack. That is a warning for vaccine design. A vaccine that cuts symptoms without blocking growth might, in theory, select for more harmful strains. The paper does not claim this has happened. It shows the risk is real enough that malaria programs should track parasite change as vaccines roll out.
plos-pbio-0020330:
Konrad P. Körding, Izumi Fukunaga, Ian S. Howard, and their team applied economics logic to movement in PLOS Biology in 2004. In economics, a utility function scores how much each outcome is worth. The authors ask whether the brain, while controlling a reach or a step, acts as if it used such a score.

By studying how people adjust to forces and errors, they infer the hidden costs the motor system seems to weigh, like effort and accuracy. If movement follows a utility rule, then many odd habits of motion fall into place. The approach also gives engineers a principled way to model human control. That helps prosthetics and robots that must move with people, not just near them.
plos-pone-0000130:
Nicholas Valmas and Paul R. Ebert published this pest control study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It compares fumigants, gases used to kill insects in stored grain, along with a phosphine booster. To run the tests safely, the authors built a new containment chamber for making concentrated phosphine gas.

Phosphine is effective but dangerous to handle, and insects keep evolving resistance to it. The authors measure how toxic the fumigants and the booster are under controlled conditions. Safer, well-measured testing helps the grain industry protect stored harvests while keeping workers safe and staying ahead of resistant pests.
plos-pone-0000230:
Bernard Le Foll, Carrie Wertheim, and Steven R. Goldberg published this addiction study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Tobacco is clearly addictive in humans. Yet experts long argued over whether nicotine by itself makes laboratory animals work to get more, as truly addictive drugs do. The authors tested nicotine's reinforcing power in non-human primates.

The title states the result: nicotine showed high reinforcing efficacy in the primates, meaning the animals worked hard to obtain it. That settles a long controversy in the authors' favor: nicotine alone can drive drug-seeking. The finding underpins tobacco regulation and the design of quitting aids.
plos-pone-0000330:
Sophie Agaugué, Laure Perrin-Cocon, Patrice André, and colleagues published this hepatitis C study in PLOS ONE in 2007. The hepatitis C virus travels in blood partly as lipo-viro-particles, virus joined with fat particles. Using particles from chronically infected patients, the authors show they interfere with TLR4 signaling in dendritic cells, damping an immune alarm pathway.

A virus that quiets the alarm can persist for decades, as hepatitis C does. The paper identifies one of its silencing tricks in real patient material. Understanding that interference helps explain chronic infection and suggests where therapies might restore the alarm.
plos-pone-0000430:
Lilian Ricaud and colleagues exposed the plant Arabidopsis to gamma rays and mapped its responses, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Gamma rays damage DNA, and plants, which cannot flee radiation, must repair or adapt. The team tracked ATM-mediated responses: ATM is a master protein that senses DNA damage and switches on defense programs, in both gene activity and development.

Arabidopsis is the standard lab plant, so its damage responses stand in for those of crops and wild plants. Knowing which genes ATM controls after irradiation helps explain how plants survive radiation in soil and seed. The work also feeds space biology, where radiation is a constant hazard for growing food.
plos-pone-0000530:
Richard P. Meisel and Stephen W. Schaeffer tracked how fruit fly chromosome arrangements pass through egg formation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila pseudoobscura carries chromosomal arrangements, flipped segments called inversions, whose frequencies vary in nature. The team studied meiotic transmission: whether arrangements are passed on fairly or gain an edge during meiosis.

Unfair transmission, called meiotic drive, can spread a chromosome variant even if it harms the fly. Testing for drive explains otherwise puzzling patterns in wild populations. Inversions in this species are a classic system from the early days of population genetics. Modern transmission tests refine what the pioneers could only infer.
plos-pone-0000630:
Joanne Miles, Jennifer A. Mitchell, Lyubomira Chakalova and colleagues mapped gene activity around the human beta-globin locus for PLOS ONE in 2007. The locus holds the globin genes used to build hemoglobin. Strong links were already known between transcription, the copying of DNA into RNA, and chemical marks on histones, the proteins DNA wraps around.

Using a method called RNA FISH in red-blood-cell precursors, the team showed copying also runs through the stretches between genes. They tracked how that intergenic transcription and the locus's epigenetic profile change with the cell cycle and development. The picture is of a whole region switching on in a coordinated, timed way.
plos-pone-0000730:
Esmeralda A. J. M. Soares, André F. A. Santos, Thatiana M. Sousa and colleagues compared how two HIV subtypes gain drug resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Subtype C is the most prevalent HIV-1 form worldwide, dominating countries with the highest HIV rates. Few studies, though, had evaluated how antiretroviral therapy performs against it. Southern Brazil was the first developing region to offer free, universal therapy.

That setting lets the authors compare resistance acquisition in subtypes B and C under real treatment programmes. If subtypes resist differently, treatment guidelines written for subtype B may fit subtype C poorly. The comparison matters most where subtype C is common and resources are thin.
plos-pone-0000830:
Anne Bergeron, Mahdi Belcaid, Grieg F. Steward and colleagues offered a divide-and-conquer plan for sequencing whole microbial communities. In environmental sequencing projects, DNA from an entire community is fragmented and sequenced, with goals including reconstructing partial or complete genomes of its members. In communities rich in species, a large fraction of the data resists assembly, because similar fragments from many species tangle together.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE method enriches the data by splitting the problem into parts it can handle. Ocean and soil samples hold most of Earth's microbes, almost none cultured. Better assembly turns raw fragments into genomes, letting science name and study organisms it cannot grow.
plos-pone-0000930:
Anna Okvist, Sofia Johansson, Alexander Kuzmin and colleagues studied a gene control system in the brains of people with alcohol dependence, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Long term drinking reshapes the brain, and those changes involve many genes at once. The NF-kappaB family of factors switches whole sets of genes on and off.

The team asked whether that system is dysregulated, thrown off balance, in chronic alcoholics. Changes there could help explain lasting cognitive problems tied to drinking. Brain tissue studies like this are hard to do and rarely direct. They still offer the closest look at what years of alcohol do inside the human brain.
plos-pone-0001030:
Satoru Yamagishi, Yoshihisa Koyama, Taiichi Katayama and colleagues built a cell model of inclusion bodies seen in inherited ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In familial ALS tied to mutant SOD1, neurons and astrocytes grow hyaline inclusions, glassy clumps holding the faulty protein. How those clumps form was not known.

The team induced similar inclusions in vitro by stressing the cell's protein handling system, in cells carrying the ALS linked mutation. A lab model lets researchers test what starts clumping and what might stop it. Inclusions are a visible mark of the disease process, so a model of their birth is a useful tool.
plos-pone-0001130:
Diseases move at different speeds in a mouse and in a human, and body size is part of the reason. Jessica Cable, Brian Enquist, and Melanie Moses took up this scaling problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article on the allometry of host-pathogen interactions. Allometry is the study of how body traits change with size.

The authors examine how body size and metabolic rate shape the pace of infection and disease progression across species. That matters for epidemiology and for a practical worry in medicine: how to translate results from small lab animals to people. A sound scaling rule makes animal studies more useful.
plos-pone-0001230:
Nigersaurus taqueti was a sauropod dinosaur that fed at ground level, cropping low plants like a lawn mower. Paul Sereno and colleagues described its skull from Early Cretaceous fossils in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The fossils document, for the first time, the cranial anatomy of a rebbachisaurid sauropod, Nigersaurus's family.

Its adaptations for ground-level herbivory are extreme: a wide, squared-off muzzle and batteries of small teeth among them. The authors argue these features challenge current ideas about feeding function and strategy among sauropods. Nigersaurus has become a textbook example of how far a plant-eating dinosaur's skull could specialize.
plos-pone-0001330:
Dental pulp from animals infected with prion diseases can carry infectivity, raising a worry for dentistry. Nadège Bourvis and colleagues assessed the risk of transmitting sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in endodontic practice, root canal work, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The concern is that the disease could spread to patients through reused instruments when prion inactivation is inadequate.

The authors model that risk in the absence of adequate prion inactivation. Prions resist standard sterilization, which makes the question more than theoretical. Their assessment helps dental regulators weigh single-use instruments and cleaning standards.
plos-pone-0001430:
Daniela Contu and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the roots of people on the island of Sardinia. The island has high rates of some immune ills, such as type 1 diabetes. Knowing its gene past is key to sound disease gene hunts there. The team read markers on the male Y chromosome across the island.

Their data point to roots that predate farming on the island. The people look gene alike in some ways, yet diverse in others. That mix shapes how gene scans should be planned there. It also adds a chapter to the tale of how island peoples formed in Europe.
plos-pone-0001530:
Xinhua Yu and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a DNA variant and multiple sclerosis. This ill harms nerve fibers, and risk runs in part through families. A variant in the DNA of the cell power units had been eyed as a risk factor. The team tested it in six European case control groups.

They report the variant does raise the risk of the disease in their data. A power unit link fits the nerve harm, since nerves hunger for energy. Each firm risk variant adds a clue to how the ill starts. It also helps sort which patients share a common root cause.
plos-pone-0001630:
Augustin Zoungrana, Boubacar Coulibaly, Ali Sié, and their co-authors ran a clinical trial in Burkina Faso on a new pairing of malaria drugs. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article tested methylene blue combined with either artesunate or amodiaquine against uncomplicated falciparum malaria. The team looked at both safety and how well the treatment worked.

Existing drug pairs based on artemisinin are the standard cure, but safe, effective, and cheap backups are still needed as the parasite adapts. Methylene blue was the first man-made malaria drug ever used, and newer studies had hinted it could help again. The full text gives the trial design, the patient results, and the side effects seen. Trials like this tell health programs which drug pairs deserve wider use.
plos-pone-0001730:
Julia J. Day, James A. Cotton, and Timothy G. Barraclough studied how cichlid fishes multiplied in Lake Tanganyika in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Why some groups and regions hold far more species than others is a basic question in evolutionary biology. Answering it needs densely sampled family trees and good study systems. The lake's cichlids, famous for their variety, offer both.

The authors examined the tempo and mode of diversification: how fast new species arose, and whether the pace changed over time. The full text gives the family tree, the timing estimates, and the pattern of bursts or steady growth. Lake radiations like this are natural tests of how new species form, and Tanganyika is the oldest of the great African lakes.
plos-pone-0001830:
Michael L. Clawson, Juergen A. Richt, Thierry Baron, and their co-authors tested cattle genes for links to atypical mad cow disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathies are recently recognized prion diseases of cattle. They are rare, with about 30 cases identified worldwide at the time.

The team tested prion gene haplotypes, inherited variants of PRNP, for an association with atypical BSE and report an association. The full text gives the cattle cases and the haplotype statistics. If certain PRNP types predispose cattle to spontaneous prion disease, surveillance and breeding programs gain a genetic risk marker for a feared food-safety disease.
plos-pone-0001930:
David Whitaker, Dennis Levi, and Graeme Kennedy tested how the eye judges a change in a moving object's path, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Vision guides how we reach for, catch, or dodge things in motion. A key skill is spotting when a moving object veers off its line, by even a small amount.

The team measured how well people spot that veer, and how the skill builds as the object is watched over time. Their title gives the theme: what the eye gleans across time sets how fine the judgment can be. Results of this sort ground models of motion vision used in science and in display design.
plos-pone-0002030:
Ali Kinkhabwala and Calin Guet shuffled gene switches to crack their code, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A promoter is the DNA stretch that sets when a gene turns on, by adding up signals from many binding proteins. Reading that code at single promoters is key to grasping how cell networks are wired.

The pair built synthetic promoters by shuffling parts, then watched how each mix behaved. Shuffled versions act as controlled tests of the code, free of the clutter of natural genes. Rules learned this way can guide the design of gene circuits with set behavior.
plos-pone-0002130:
Maria Tsirigotis, Mitchell Baldwin, Matthew Tang, and co-authors traced a cell signal that worsens damage from faulty proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some brain diseases are caused by proteins with an expanded stretch of the amino acid glutamine, called polyglutamine repeats. How these proteins kill cells was not well understood when the study began.

The team showed that the harm from expanded polyglutamine proteins runs mainly through a stress signal switch called p38MAPK. Blocking that pathway reduced the cell damage in their tests. The work points to a possible drug target for a group of diseases that includes Huntington's disease. In those diseases, slowing cell death would matter a great deal.
plos-pone-0002230:
Laith Abu-Raddad, Amalia Magaret, Connie Celum, and co-authors weighed the role of genital herpes in Africa's HIV epidemic, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Observational studies had long suggested that herpes simplex virus type 2, the usual cause of genital herpes, helps HIV spread. At the time, herpes vaccines were in development and trials were testing whether treating herpes with acyclovir could slow HIV.

The authors assessed how large a share of HIV infections herpes may have driven. They conclude herpes played a bigger part than any other sexually transmitted infection in raising HIV prevalence in Africa. That ranking shapes where prevention money can do the most work.
plos-pone-0002330:
Matthias Möllenbeck and co-authors followed the path a ciliate takes to unscramble one of its genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some single-celled ciliates rebuild their genomes as they develop a working nucleus. In the process, internal eliminated sequences are cut out and the coding pieces of genes, sometimes stored in scrambled order, are rejoined.

The team traced the pathway used to detangle a scrambled gene step by step. A cell that can cut, shuffle, and reseal its own DNA with precision performs a feat of natural editing. Understanding its rules informs both genome evolution and the design of DNA-based computing.
plos-pone-0002430:
In 2008, Lynn and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Francis C. Lynn, Lidia Sanchez, Ramon Gomis, and others. Its subject is identification of the bHLH Factor Math6 as a Novel Component of the Embryonic Pancreas Transcriptional Network. Basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors play important roles in differentiation processes during embryonic development of vertebrates.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002530:
A research team led by Owusu-Agyei reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Seth Owusu-Agyei, Kwaku Poku Asante, Ruth Owusu, and others. Its subject is an Open Label, Randomised Trial of Artesunate+Amodiaquine, Artesunate+Chlorproguanil-Dapsone and Artemether-Lumefantrine for the Treatment of Uncomplicated Malaria. Artesunate+amodiaquine (AS+AQ) and artemether-lumefantrine (AL) are now the most frequently recommended first line treatments for uncomplicated malaria in Africa.

Artesunate+chlorproguanil-dapsone (AS+CD) was a potential alternative for treatment of uncomplicated malaria. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002630:
Ursula Schwab led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was triacylglycerol fatty acid composition in Diet-Induced weight loss in subjects with abnormal glucose metabolism – the GENOBIN study. Authorship is credited in the record to Ursula Schwab and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The effect of weight loss on different plasma lipid subclasses at the molecular level is unknown. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002730:
Tatiana N. Badaeva led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was genetic variation and de novo mutations in the parthenogenetic caucasian rock lizard darevskia unisexualis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Tatiana N. Badaeva, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Unisexual all-female lizards of the genus Darevskia that are well adapted to various habitats are known to reproduce normally by true parthenogenesis. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002830:
Jeffrey A. Lyon led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was protection induced by plasmodium falciparum MSP1 42 is Strain-Specific, antigen and adjuvant dependent, and correlates with antibody responses. The catalog record names Jeffrey A. Lyon first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Vaccination with Plasmodium falciparum MSP1 42 /complete Freund's adjuvant (FA) followed by MSP1 42 /incomplete FA is the only known regimen that protects Aotus. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002930:
Nathan Morrell, Philipp Leucht, Ludan Zhao and co-authors found a way to deliver Wnt protein in the body in 2008. Wnt signals drive strong growth and repair effects that could have real medical value. Yet there were no specific Wnt boosters and no method to deliver purified Wnt protein in a living animal.

Wnt proteins carry lipid tags needed for their activity, which makes them hard to handle. Packaging Wnt in liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, kept it active, as the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, that step opens tests of Wnt therapy for repair in living tissue.
plos-pone-0003030:
Esteban Gurzov, Fernanda Ortis, Latifa Bakiri and co-authors studied the factor JunB in pancreatic beta cells in 2008. In type 1 diabetes, cytokines help drive beta cell death by rewiring gene networks. The AP-1 transcription factor family is a key regulator of inflammation and cell death in that setting.

The team evaluated JunB, one AP-1 subunit. Its title-level finding is that JunB inhibits endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis in beta cells. Published in PLOS ONE, a protective factor inside insulin-making cells is a candidate worth guarding in early diabetes. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003130: Pradeep K. Gupta and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on anthrax lethal factor, one of the toxins of the anthrax bacterium. The title states its narrow question: what role the amino acids at the start of the protein play in how potent the toxin is. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no findings are stated here.
plos-pone-0003230:
Lidia Ruiz, Magali Traskine, Irene Ferrer and colleagues characterize the p53 response to senescence in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. P53 activation can trigger various outcomes, among them reversible growth arrest or cellular senescence, the permanent stop of division. It is a live debate whether these outcomes are influenced by quantitative or qualitative mechanisms. The relative contribution of p53 to Ras-induced senescence is also at issue.

Readers follow an attempt to define what kind of p53 response a stress signal produces. Senescence is a barrier against cancer, so its triggers matter for therapy. Knowing whether dose or quality decides the outcome changes how drugs might be used.
plos-pone-0003330:
Paul E. Dux and René Marois study the attentional blink in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The attentional blink is the impaired ability to detect the second of two targets. The targets appear in a rapid serial visual presentation stream of distractors. The blink occurs if the second target appears within two hundred to six hundred milliseconds of the first. The team examined whether the ability to inhibit distractors predicts this effect.

The title reports that distractor inhibition predicts individual differences in the attentional blink. Readers learn why some people miss the second target far more than others. Individual differences can reveal the mechanism behind a classic attention limit.
plos-pone-0007430:
Chetan Hans and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how high blood fats damage blood vessels and the nerves that regulate them. They used mice lacking the ApoE gene and fed them a high-fat diet, a standard model of artery disease. The question was whether a DNA-repair enzyme called PARP-1 helps drive the damage.

Mice without PARP-1 were protected against much of the harm. Their blood vessels worked better, and their autonomic nerve control stayed steadier. The protection involved eNOS, an enzyme that keeps vessels relaxed, and lower oxidative stress. The results suggest that blocking PARP-1 could shield vessels from fat-driven injury. That idea may matter for diseases where cholesterol harms both arteries and nerves.
plos-pone-0007530:
Hiroyuki Nakagawa and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Lasp-2, a protein that grips the cell's actin skeleton. Lasp-2 gathers in actin bundles and at focal adhesions, the anchor points where cells grip their surroundings. The protein has three structural regions. Which regions do the gripping was unknown. The team tested the LIM domain and the nebulin-repeat region in particular.

Both regions proved to contribute to the interaction. They help Lasp-2 bind actin filaments and settle into focal adhesions. Knowing the division of labor explains how the protein organizes cell shape. Actin anchors underlie movement, division, and a cell's sense of place. A protein that manages those anchors matters in development and in cancer spread. The study assigns its parts their jobs.
plos-pone-0007630:
Dhruv Sareen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 with a safety warning for stem cell medicine. Growing human neural progenitor cells in dishes is the foundation of future cell therapies for the brain. Such therapies need cells with a normal chromosome set. Abnormal cells raise the risk of tumors after transplant. The team checked the chromosomes of cultured human neural progenitor cells over time.

During culture, some cells gained an extra copy of chromosome 7 and of chromosome 19. Those trisomies appeared as the cells expanded in vitro. A therapy grown from such cells could carry hidden danger. The warning matters now, before these cells reach patients widely. Routine chromosome checks should accompany long culture. The study is a guardrail for a promising field: growth in a dish must not quietly rewrite the genome.
plos-pone-0007730:
Yuan-Ping Pang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports a new drug candidate against botulinum neurotoxin serotype A. That toxin causes botulism, a life-threatening paralysis. Current antibody treatments can only catch toxin still outside nerve cells.

Once the toxin slips inside, antibodies cannot reach it. The active part is an enzyme that cuts key proteins. The team used computer-aided design, then built the molecule they designed. The result is a potent small-molecule blocker of that enzyme. Such a drug could treat poisoning after exposure, not just prevent it.
plos-pone-0007830:
Massimiliano Baldassarre and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies filamins, proteins that link the cell's actin skeleton to its surface. Mammals have three filamins, and the founding member, FLNa, was tied to cell migration. Mutations in FLNA cause a brain disorder where neurons fail to migrate.

The authors tested how filamins control the first steps of movement. Filamins regulate how cells spread on a surface. They also govern how migration gets started. Those early steps decide much of what follows. The findings matter for development and for cancer spread.
plos-pone-0007930:
Hong Choi and colleagues named a new player in bone control in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is Lrp4, found on osteoblasts, the cells that build bone. They showed it acts as a receptor, a docking site, for two known bone signals, Dickkopf 1 and sclerostin.

Tests in living mice linked Lrp4 to both bone growth and bone turnover, the steady renewal of the skeleton. When this docking step fails, the balance of building and breakdown shifts. The finding adds a handle for research on weak bones and on drugs that aim to strengthen them.
plos-pone-0008030:
Takehiko Ogura and colleagues gave the silkworm its first full Ras gene survey in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ras proteins are growth switches found in nearly all complex life, famed for their role in human cancer. In most insects, the family had barely been charted.

The team found three Ras genes in the silkworm and read where and when each one works. The silkworm is both a farm animal and a lab model, so the survey serves two masters. It also lets scientists compare the insect switches with the human ones that go wrong in tumors.
plos-pone-0008130:
Manuela Basso and colleagues cataloged the proteins locked in clumps in ALS tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009. ALS kills the nerve cells that run muscles, and clumps of protein are a hallmark in those cells. Which proteins fill the clumps, and why they gather, stayed murky.

The stubborn clump proteins, washed free of all that dissolves, pointed to nitrative stress, a form of chemical damage from nitrogen-based radicals. The damage looks like a cause of the gathering, not a side effect. That chain gives drug hunters a place to cut in, before clumps form.
plos-pone-0008230:
Patrick D. Schloss presented a DNA sequence aligner in PLOS ONE in 2009 for microbial ecology. Surveys of microbes keep growing as sequencing capacity grows. Analysis then hits a bottleneck: building a meaningful multiple sequence alignment. Common aligners differ in quality and speed. A poor alignment can distort every later conclusion about a community.

Schloss offered a high-throughput tool built for these large surveys. Faster, reliable alignment lets researchers handle far more sequences. That helps studies of bacteria in soil, water, and the human body. The paper is a practical methods contribution for a fast-growing field.
plos-pone-0008330:
Paul Zak and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how a hormone can change how kind men are. How we choose to be kind or to act for self is a deep point in the study of acts. The team gave the male hormone testosterone to 25 men. Each man took both the drug and a fake drug at set times, and no one knew which was which at the time. Blood tests checked that the hormone did rise as planned.

Kind acts were scored with a trade game in which one man splits cash and the next can turn the split down. Men on the hormone gave less in the game than men on the fake. A body-made drug thus swung a choice of cash and kind acts in a clear way. The work links the body's own drugs to day-to-day social choice.
plos-pone-0008430:
Xiaolong Wang, Deming Gou, and Shuang-yong Xu present a lab method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their method makes short bits of DNA called antisense oligonucleotides. Such bits can block small RNAs or their targets. Labs use them as tools, and doctors may one day use them as drugs. But bits made by chemists often hold flawed copies that are hard to remove.

The method, called PEAR, uses two enzymes to copy and cut DNA in a loop. It can make large amounts of clean product in the lab. The paper shows how the loop works and why purity improves. That could lower cost for research use.
plos-pone-0008530:
Christine Bell and co-authors track two factors in early mouse embryos in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The factors are SNAI1 and SNAI2. They initiate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions in development and cancer spread. Those transitions let stationary cells become mobile ones. The team find both factors expressed in preimplantation embryos. Their pattern at the two-cell stage is asymmetric, meaning uneven between cells.

Later, the factors become segregated to the trophectoderm in the blastocyst. The trophectoderm is the outer layer that forms the placenta. This segregation hints at an early role in lineage choice. The work reveals an unexpected place for these transition factors.
plos-pone-0008630:
Josephine V. J. Lightowler, Graham S. Cooke, Portia Mutevedzi, and colleagues reported a clinical study from South Africa in PLOS ONE in 2010. It deals with cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal infection of the membranes around the brain. Among people with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa, few illnesses kill more of them. The study site was KwaZulu-Natal province.

More patients there were gaining access to drugs that fight HIV itself. Yet surviving also depended on how well the meningitis was treated. So the team examined which patient and care factors were linked to how cases turned out. Their findings show where local treatment fell short. They also point to changes that could help more patients live.
plos-pone-0008730:
Azad Kumar, Elisa Greggio, Alexandra Beilina, and colleagues tested the aim of a Parkinson-linked enzyme. Their work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mutations in LRRK2 are the most common known cause of inherited Parkinson disease. LRRK2 is a kinase, an enzyme that tags proteins with phosphate. One possible target is 4E-BP, a protein that controls protein making. Whether LRRK2 truly tags it was disputed.

In test-tube assays, the enzyme tagged itself far more strongly than 4E-BP. That weak aim casts doubt on 4E-BP as a natural target. Clearing up false targets saves Parkinson research from dead ends.
plos-pone-0008830:
Eric Wooten, Lakshmanan Iyer, Maria Claudia Montefusco, and colleagues used gene networks to find suspects for a heart defect. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bicuspid aortic valve has two flaps instead of three. The defect runs strongly in families. Only about one person in a hundred has it, limiting classic gene hunts. The team instead preselected promising gene variants.

Network-guided analysis flagged variant patterns in AXIN1, PDIA2, and endoglin. Those patterns tracked with the valve defect. Smart preselection can rescue studies of rare traits. The suspects now await confirmation in larger groups.
plos-pone-0008930:
Brett Zani, Laura Indolfi, and Elazer Edelman described tiny tubes linking airway cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cells they studied line the bronchi, the air passages inside the lungs. Cells often talk by sending signals through body fluids over long distances. They can also touch directly when they sit side by side.

Under the microscope, the team saw bronchial cells grow thin bridges toward each other. Cells used these tubes to move and to pass signals between neighbours. The bridges formed a direct line of contact that fluid signals cannot match. Such links may help the airway lining repair itself after injury.
plos-pone-0009030:
Sumanti Gupta and co-authors watched a fungus attack chickpea plants at the earliest moment, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fusarium oxysporum causes wilt disease that devastates chickpea crops. Plants often resist invaders by killing their own cells around the entry point. Wounding the plant lets this fungus in, starting the contest.

Rather than the defence burst coming first, the fungus struck the plant's core metabolism. Basic processes that keep the plant's cells running were its initial target. That early hit may weaken the plant before defences can organise. Crop breeders could use the timing to build chickpeas that react faster.
plos-pone-0009130:
Ido Yosef and co-authors starved E. coli of its protein-delivery crew and watched membranes suffer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Membrane proteins must be built straight into the cell's membrane. A delivery system called SRP guides them there as they are made. Two parts, Ffh and FtsY, are each essential in this bacterium.

The team drained each part in turn and tracked membrane protein production. Some earlier work had hinted the system might be partly optional. Depletion confirmed the SRP route as central to membrane biogenesis. The result firms up a basic chapter of bacterial cell biology.
plos-pone-0009230:
Kim Brolin, Kristina Persson, Mats Wahlgren, and co-authors published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria parasites that infect pregnant women can pile up in the placenta. A parasite surface protein called VAR2CSA drives that pile-up. Women pregnant for the first time are hit hardest, while mothers in later pregnancies often carry protective antibodies.

The team studied how those natural antibodies recognize different parts of VAR2CSA. They used samples from pregnant women in a malaria-endemic area. Knowing which parts of the protein antibodies actually target is vital for a vaccine. A pregnancy malaria vaccine would need to copy the protection that repeated pregnancies build naturally.
plos-pone-0009330:
Paul Azzopardi and co-authors published this mineral study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Osteopontin is a protein that blocks the growth of hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone and teeth. In dishes it stops crystals from forming and growing. In the body it is thought to keep soft tissues from hardening with mineral.

The team studied how osteopontin interacts with the crystal surface. They weighed the roles of electric charge and of the protein's shape in that grip. Details matter because the same control system fails in diseases of unwanted calcification. The study separates two forces that earlier work had lumped together.
plos-pone-0011430:
Hedley Grantham, Robert Pressey, and Jessie Wells tested in 2010 how well conservation shortcuts actually work. Planners cannot map every species, so they protect areas rich in a few well-known groups and assume the rest of life is covered. Earlier tests of that assumption disagreed wildly, and the team asked why the verdict kept changing.

They found that the answer depends on which measure of success is chosen, producing a kaleidoscope of different results from the same plans. A reserve network can look excellent by one yardstick and poor by another. The humbling lesson is that planners must state their yardstick openly and test several. Otherwise a protected map may guard only the stand-in species while the life it was meant to represent slips away uncounted.
plos-pone-0011530:
Susanna Marg and co-authors characterized in 2010 a mouse whose cell glue cannot grip properly. Vinculin is a protein that anchors cells to their surroundings by binding actin, the cell's cable protein, at adhesion sites. The mouse carries a splice variant of vinculin, missing two segments, that is produced constantly and cannot bind actin at all.

Studying what breaks in such a mouse reveals, by subtraction, exactly what the grip does for tissues under mechanical load. Heart, skin, and vessels all pull on their cells, and weak anchoring shows first where the pulling is hardest. The mutant is a precise tool rather than a curiosity: one defined defect, present from birth, in a protein found in nearly every tissue. Cell biologists can use it to test which adhesion jobs truly need vinculin's grip and which have backups.
plos-pone-0011630:
Steven Cannon and colleagues revisited the deep history of legume plants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Legumes, including beans and peas, host soil bacteria in root nodules and gain nitrogen from the air. Evidence suggested the whole legume genome doubled early in their history, and many assumed that doubling came before the nodule partnership.

The authors tested that order across legume groups. They found the doubling did not predate nodulation in all lineages, so the partnership arose without waiting for it everywhere. The revised timeline changes the standard story of how one of farming's most valuable plant alliances began.
plos-pone-0011730:
Ruolin Yang and Bing Su compared gene teamwork in human and mouse tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2010. High-throughput tools now let scientists watch many genes at once. While many single genes behind species differences have been characterised, far less is known about how whole tissue-level gene groups evolved.

Yang and Su identified modules of genes tied to specific tissues in each species and compared them side by side. Some teamwork proved conserved, while other modules were rewired between human and mouse. Knowing which networks stayed stable warns against assuming mouse results always transfer to human biology.
plos-pone-0011830:
Carlos Caicedo-Carvajal, Troy Shinbrot, and Ramsey Foty published this 2010 study on how groups of cells change from flowing masses into firm tissue. Growing embryos and healing wounds both need cells that can first move past each other, then settle and hold still. The team focused on bonds between two proteins, integrin and fibronectin, that link cells to the material around them.

Working with three-dimensional clumps of cells, the authors show that the strength of those integrin and fibronectin bonds decides whether a clump behaves like a thick liquid or like a soft solid. Weak bonding lets cells keep trading places, while strong bonding locks the group in place. That switch helps explain how a loose crowd of cells becomes stable, organized tissue.
plos-pone-0011930:
Subhadip Raychaudhuri proposed in 2010 a stripped-down model of how cells decide to die. Real signaling networks are large, but the essential logic of sensing a stimulus and adapting to it can be captured in a minimal network. The model was built to respond in proportion to signals of different strengths.

Applied to apoptosis, the cell's orderly death program, the model explains why genetically identical cells facing the same signal do not all die at once. Random differences between cells emerge naturally from the network's structure. A simple model that reproduces that variability gives researchers a test bed for ideas about drug resistance, where a few cancer cells survive treatment that kills the rest.
plos-pone-0012030:
Roger Chung and co-workers reported in 2010 that a natural metal-handling protein can stop amyloid clumping driven by copper. Alzheimer's disease is marked by insoluble plaques of beta-amyloid, and evidence suggests copper and zinc help the amyloid aggregate. The protein tested was metallothionein, the main human protein that binds copper and zinc for safekeeping.

In rat cortical neurons, metallothionein blocked the copper-driven aggregation of amyloid and its toxicity. A built-in defense that neutralizes the metal trigger is an appealing lead: rather than attacking plaques after they form, boosting this guard could prevent the clumping chemistry from starting. The work also ties brain metal balance more firmly to Alzheimer's damage.
plos-pone-0012130:
Brad Reynolds, Sean Powers, and Mary Anne Bishop tracked fish around built and natural reefs in Alaska's Prince William Sound, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Damage to nearshore habitat has pushed many groups to build artificial reefs, hoping fish will settle there. Copper rockfish and lingcod are key fish in this sound, and both were fitted into the study using sound-based tracking tags.

The tags let the team follow where each fish stayed and how far it roamed, at created sites and natural ones alike. Knowing whether fish truly live at built reefs, or just pass through, decides whether reef building is worth the cost. The results feed into how Alaska manages habitat repair after damage.
plos-pone-0012230:
Leah Gerber, Manuela González-Suárez, Claudia Hernández-Camacho, and co-authors studied breeding California sea lions in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this mating system, males fight to hold groups of females, gaining more mates through aggression.
