Their observations during the June to August breeding season covered how both male and female behavior across that season shapes how many pups females produce.

Aggression carries a price: effort spent fighting and guarding is effort not spent elsewhere, and turmoil can cost females and pups too. Measuring that price in a wild colony tests a core claim of evolutionary theory with real animals. It also helps managers predict how disturbance at crowded breeding beaches affects the next generation.
plos-pone-0012330:
Antariksh Tyagi, Sumit Bag, Virendra Shukla, and co-authors tested a shortcut for identifying species from short DNA reads, in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA barcoding identifies a species from a snippet of a standard gene region, and it normally judges identity by genetic distance or signature characters. With snippets so short, those judgments can blur between close species.

Their approach counts how often each short word of DNA letters appears in the barcode region, a frequency fingerprint that separates species across kingdoms, from fungi to animals. A method needing only short reads works with damaged museum specimens and gut or soil samples alike. Faster, cheaper identification feeds everything from food fraud detection to biodiversity surveys.
plos-pone-0012430:
Giuseppe Nicastro, Sokol Todi, Ezgi Karaca and colleagues dissected the working head of the ataxin-3 protein, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ataxin-3 faults cause Machado-Joseph disease, a brain disorder that steals movement control. The protein normally trims ubiquitin chains, the tags that mark other proteins for disposal, and its Josephin domain does the gripping and cutting.

The team mapped how the domain binds ubiquitin chains and where it cuts them. Those details explain how the healthy protein works and what may misfire in disease. A clear map of the cutting head helps chemists think about drugs that could tune its activity in patients.
plos-pone-0012630:
Lee, Singh, Tsark and co-authors altered a control region that keeps two growth genes apart in mice. The genes H19 and Igf2 sit side by side, and a boundary element works only on the copy from the mother. There, a protein called CTCF blocks distant enhancers from reaching the Igf2 promoter.

Their 2010 change made the boundary work on both copies at once. Pups then grew poorly before birth and many died around delivery. The harsh outcome shows how fine the balance of this gene pair is, and why its faults appear in human growth disorders.
plos-pone-0012730:
Benn, Weaver, Billet and co-authors mapped how much of the deep North East Atlantic seafloor humans have touched. Most past checks stopped at waters shallower than two hundred metres. Their 2010 assessment went deeper, tallying fishing, cables, litter and other marks across a wide ocean area.

Knowing the true footprint is the first step to protecting deep habitats that recover very slowly. Trawling and other deep uses were still growing when they wrote. Their map gives regulators a baseline against which later damage or recovery can be judged.  Deep sea floors hold species found nowhere else on earth.
plos-pone-0012830:
Hanson and Ballantyne tested whether the colour of dried blood can betray how long a stain has sat at a scene. Knowing when blood was shed would fix the time frame of a crime for investigators. Their 2010 study tracked the hemoglobin Soret band, a strong light-absorption feature of blood pigment, as stains aged.

The band shifted toward blue wavelengths as time since deposition grew. A steady shift tied to age could turn a bloodstain into a rough clock. Forensic teams would still need care with heat and light effects.
pmc-2631630:
Spek reviews the state of structure validation in chemical crystallography in 2009. Crystallographers build atomic models from diffraction data, and journals publish thousands each year. A model can look plausible yet still contain errors that mislead later work.

Validation means testing a reported structure against checks for geometry, fit, and internal consistency. Spek, known for widely used checking software, sums up current practice and its gaps. Stronger routine checks protect chemistry and materials science, since one flawed structure can waste other teams' experiments and misdirect drug or material design.  Journals increasingly expected such checks before accepting a new structure report.
pmc-3043330:
Schulz, Altman, and Moher present the journal version of the CONSORT 2010 statement on reporting randomised trials. The statement gives updated guidelines for reports of parallel group trials, where patients are assigned by chance to treatment or control. Clear reporting lets readers judge a trial's fairness.

The 2010 update refreshes the checklist using new evidence about bias and reporting quality. Authors must show how the trial was designed, run, and analysed. This version appeared across leading medical journals at once, underlining its role as the shared standard for trial reports. The same text appeared in several leading journals so no reader would miss it.
pmc-3632530:
McMurdie and Holmes present phyloseq, an R package for shared analysis and graphics of microbiome census data. Studying microbial communities by way of DNA sequencing brings many challenges. Work must integrate ecology, genes, species history, statistics, pictures, and testing in one single flow.

Phyloseq joins those pieces in a single environment built for sharing and repeating analyses. As study designs grew broader, a common toolkit kept results alike between labs. The package became standard equipment in microbiome science, from gut health studies to soil and ocean surveys.  Shared data forms also let ecologists and coders speak the same language.
pmc-3690530:
Scheres presents RELION, a Bayesian approach to cryo-electron microscopy structure determination. RELION is an open-source program for refining macromolecular structures from single-particle cryo-EM data. Alternative approaches often rely on user expertise to tune parameters and steer the process by hand.

A Bayesian method instead weighs many possible structures by likelihood, regularising the result to avoid overfitting noise. That statistical discipline helped cryo-EM produce reliable, near-atomic models of large complexes. RELION became a central tool in the cryo-EM revolution that reshaped structural biology.  Drug-sized complexes once beyond reach became routine targets after such software matured.
pmc-5439030:
Cohen, Brauer, Burnett, and their co-authors estimated the global burden of disease from ambient air pollution in 2017. Breathing polluted outdoor air raises illness and death rates and ranks among the top causes of disease burden worldwide. The team used data from the Global Burden of Diseases Study 2015.

They charted how deaths and disease burden tied to dirty air changed between 1990 and 2015, worldwide and country by country. Fine particles from traffic, industry, and fuel burning drive most of the harm. The trends show where cleaner air policies are winning and where exposure still rises. Such estimates press governments to treat air quality as a health priority.
pmc-5467230:
Lebreton, van der Zwet, Damsteeg, and their co-authors estimated river plastic emissions to the world's oceans in 2017. Plastics in the marine environment had become a major concern because they persist at sea. They harm marine life and potentially human health as well.

Cutting that flow first requires knowing where marine plastic comes from and how much each source adds. The team modeled how much plastic rivers carry into the oceans and which rivers contribute most. Rivers collect waste from whole inland regions, so they are natural points for intervention. Ranking them helps governments and cleanup programs target the flows where action cuts ocean plastic fastest.
pmc-5648830:
Nicholas Vogt and colleagues published this study in 2017 on the gut microbes of people with Alzheimer disease. Alzheimer disease is the most common form of dementia, and its causes are still not fully known. Animal work had hinted that gut bacteria might affect the sticky brain deposits seen in the disease.

The team compared stool samples from patients and healthy controls and found clear differences in which bacteria were present. Some bacterial groups were less common in patients, while others were more common. The results support a link between the gut and the brain in dementia, and they point to new paths for research on prevention and care.
pmc-7108130:
Xueting Yao, Fei Ye, Miao Zhang, and coauthors studied hydroxychloroquine against SARS-CoV-2 in the lab in 2020. The virus had broken out in Wuhan and spread worldwide. Chloroquine, an old malaria drug, was being tried sporadically in patients.

Hydroxychloroquine shares chloroquine's action but is generally less toxic. Cell tests showed it blocked the virus effectively. Modeling of drug levels in lung tissue suggested a dosing plan for trials. The authors presented it as a candidate to test, not a proven cure; later large trials found no benefit for patients. The dosing model was offered as a starting point for clinical trials, which later settled the question.
pmc-7839230:
Melissa Rethlefsen and colleagues introduced PRISMA-S in 2021, a reporting checklist for the literature searches behind systematic reviews. A systematic review stands or falls on its search, since a missed study can tilt the conclusions. Yet searches are often described so briefly that nobody can repeat or judge them.

PRISMA-S extends the well known PRISMA reporting statement with items specific to searching, covering databases, full search strategies, and how records were handled. The authors explain why earlier guidance left gaps and how the new items close them. The checklist gives reviewers, editors, and readers a way to see whether a review's evidence hunt was thorough enough to trust.
pmc-9186530:
Sergey Nurk, Sergey Koren, Arang Rhie, and the Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium presented in 2022 the first complete sequence of a human genome. The reference genome released in 2000 covered only the euchromatic share of our DNA, the gene rich portion that older methods could read. The remaining portion, rich in repeated sequences, stayed unfinished for two decades.

The consortium sequenced those last regions end to end, assembling a gapless genome of just over three billion letters. The new sequence adds whole stretches of DNA never read before, including regions around centromeres. A truly complete reference sharpens every use of the genome in medicine and biology, from variant hunting to understanding how chromosomes behave.
pmc-9931230:
Tiffany Kung, Morgan Cheatham, and colleagues tested in 2023 how well ChatGPT, a large language model, could perform on the United States Medical Licensing Exam. The licensing exam has three parts, taken across medical school and early training, and it sets the bar for practicing medicine in the United States. The team fed the exam questions to the model without any specialized training or help.

They report that ChatGPT scored at or close to the passing line on all three parts. That result landed early in the public life of such models and drew wide attention. The authors discuss what it could mean for medical education, including both the promise of AI study support and the questions it raises about assessment.
plos-pone-0359630:

Named RCTE, it is a piece of AI software, an object detection framework that sorts what it finds into many classes. Object detection software draws attention to specific findings in an image and labels what they are. A framework built for dental panoramas must handle crowded, overlapping teeth and varied problems in one scan. Dentists and imaging researchers could use such tools as a second set of eyes, and this work adds one more candidate system to compare.

The team draws on three kinds of samples: ancient, historical, and modern, spanning a long stretch of the species' past and present.

Comparing DNA across eras shows how bat populations have changed in size and connection over time. Museum specimens and old remains let genetics reach back before modern surveys began. Wildlife agencies deciding how to protect a scarce bat need this long view to judge whether today's populations are shrinking or holding steady.
plos-pone-0358130:
Jae Ho Shim, Ji Yeon Lee, Jihye Han, and Hyeon Soo Kim published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns muscle wasting during spaceflight, where weightlessness weakens astronauts. A blood-accessible biomarker panel would let flight surgeons track muscle loss with a blood draw instead of scans or biopsies. Genes whose activity can be read in blood and that change over time suit the longitudinal monitoring the title describes. Space medicine teams planning long missions are the readers who need such a simple tracking tool.
plos-pone-0355130:
Gang Zhou, Shishi Liao, and Qi Jiang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on wireless power transfer, sending electricity without cables. The system design is called LCC-S, one layout of compensating circuits. Working from an equivalent circuit model, the authors carry out multi-objective parameter design, tuning several goals at once.

Pareto analysis then maps the trade-offs, showing which designs cannot improve one goal without losing on another. Wireless charging designers must balance power, efficiency, and size, so a trade-off map is more honest than a single best answer. Engineers building charging pads and vehicle systems are the readers for this design method.
plos-pone-0359530: Hormenu and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on heart and metabolic health in Cape Coast, Ghana. plos-pone-0359330:
Guy Rubin and three colleagues report a small laboratory test of a new enzyme treatment for Dupuytren's disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease builds collagen rich cords in the hand that slowly pull fingers into a bent position. An injected bacteria made collagenase already treats it without surgery, and the team asked whether a lab made version of a related enzyme could do the same job.

They took cords removed during surgery from five patients, injected the test enzyme or a plain buffer, and pulled the tissue apart on a measuring machine. Enzyme treated cords tore under clearly less force, roughly a third lower in this tiny series. The authors call it early proof of concept and say dose, timing, and safety work must come before any patient use.
