The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7773630: Bhaskaran and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on HIV infection and COVID-19 death: a population-based (covering a whole population) cohort analysis of UK primary care data and linked national death. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8168830: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on framework for the treatment and reporting of missing data in observational studies: the treatment and reporting of missing data. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9949730: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at brazilian guidelines (official advice) of hypertension (high blood pressure) - 2020. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8371430: A 2023 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at the impact of COVID-19 lockdown on child and adolescent mental health: systematic review (a review of every study). It pulls together all the available studies on the question and grades the evidence. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc7288430: This 2020 research paper covers automated recovery, annotation and curation of germ viruses, and testing of viral community function from genomic sequences. Viruses are central to germ community structure in all environments. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
measure-for-measure-pg1530: Justice and mercy collide in this edition of Shakespeare's dark Vienna comedy, where the puritan Angelo condemns a young man for the very sin he is about to commit himself. Isabella's desperate plea and the disguised Duke's manipulations drive a plot of bed-tricks and pardons. Morally daring theater that still provokes debate.
long-odds-pg2730: H. Rider Haggard's Long Odds: an African hunting tale of desperate chances. Thrilling and brief, it shows his gift. A fine short Haggard, haggard's hunters face impossible odds, a short, sharp African tale, a short, sharp African tale well told.
the-tavern-knight-pg3030: Sabatini’s 1904 Cavalier: a king’s man in the Civil War. Swordplay and loyalty in his early style. A dashing historical romance. A dashing early Sabatini romance, a dashing early Sabatini romance, a dashing early Sabatini romance.
what-to-do-thoughts-evoked-by-the-census: Tolstoy's What to Do grew from his work on the 1882 Moscow census. Face to face with city poverty, the great novelist asks hard questions. He asks why riches and misery live side by side. A burning essay on conscience and wealth.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger collects choice quotations from a fine Gutenberg edition. The best and brightest lines stand ready here for quiet browsing. Fine wit and homely wisdom appear in small pleasing doses. A handy reader's treasury for the shelf.
plos-pone-0356630:
Zhuwen Yan and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on keeping steel strip flat during cold rolling under very high force. When a mill squeezes strip hard, ordinary roll bending controls can fail, leaving wavy edges and uneven thickness. The team studied a six-high tandem mill and replaced slow physics simulations with fast statistical stand-ins, then searched them with two optimization algorithms for the best roll bending settings.

Under the heaviest rolling force they tested, the optimized combination of work-roll and intermediate-roll bending cut the thickness variation across the strip to about a third of its former value. Surface crown errors shrank as well, pressure became far more even, and edge waves nearly disappeared. Analysis also shows how extreme force shifts the best settings, and why intermediate rolls resist certain wave defects better. The approach offers mills a route to flatter, high-strength strip.
plos-pone-0348530:
Julia Heisig and colleagues published a 2026 interview study in PLOS ONE on why German doctors order routine monitoring scans for patients with coronary heart disease or past stroke. Such check-ups, including heart and neck-artery ultrasound, aim to catch worsening disease early, yet evidence for the right tests and timing is thin. The team interviewed twenty-two doctors, general practitioners, cardiologists, and neurologists across two states, and analyzed the conversations thematically.

Doctors generally saw monitoring as beneficial, a chance to spot progression and adjust treatment in time. They also named its risks: overdiagnosis, overuse, and overtreatment when scans come too often. Motives for ordering ultrasound ranged from reassurance and safety worries to financial incentives, and doctors disagreed about whether routine scanning is justified. Many reported too little guidance on intervals. Clearer evidence on when monitoring helps, they say, would cut both missed decline and needless testing.
plos-pone-0357030:
Juan Felipe Valdés-López and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE on how the COVID-19 virus turns off a calming immune pathway. Severe COVID is driven by runaway inflammation, especially the signal interleukin 6, from immune cells called mononuclear phagocytes. The team combined gene profiles from patients' blood cells with dish-grown macrophages, and tested what the active form of vitamin D could do.

Infection switched on an inflammatory program tied to disease severity, flooding the cells with interleukin 6 and its signaling machinery. At the same time, the virus dimmed the vitamin D receptor and the genes it normally controls, leaving the cells less able to respond to vitamin D's braking effect. Adding that active vitamin D form strongly suppressed the inflammatory output in their functional tests. The findings sketch a mechanism for the cytokine storm, and why vitamin D status may matter in severe infection.
plos-pone-0355730:
Martin Ackah and colleagues build a questionnaire that measures what rest actually feels like for adults living with long-term fatiguing illness. Rest is prescribed often in rehab, yet it is poorly defined, and no tool captured its full experience. The team drafted questions with expert input, then tested them on adults with such conditions, checking structure, consistency, and links with existing coping scales.

The final scale holds a compact set of items in six themes. They cover rest habits, how restoring rest feels, and planning rest. They also cover barriers, emotions about rest, and the risk of resting too little. Several themes lined up sensibly with older coping measures. Ackah and colleagues say clinicians can now track rest quality instead of just telling patients to rest more.
plos-pone-0355830:
Maria Pérez and co-authors trace the careers of tens of thousands of United States medical school graduates to find who leaves academic medicine before reaching senior rank. Women and several minority groups remain scarce among senior faculty, and the leak points matter for fixing that. The study follows graduates appointed as junior faculty over two decades and models which traits predict early exit.

Women, Asian faculty, and underrepresented groups each left at higher rates than white male peers, as did those carrying debt or starting at the lowest rank. A year of research during residency and a research-heavy first institution both protected against leaving. Department mattered too. Pérez and colleagues argue that retention fixes must start long before promotion decisions arrive.
plos-pone-0354030:
Hongwei Li and co-authors build an AI system that cleans up underwater photographs blurred and tinted by water itself. Robots and divers need clear images, but many enhancers either invent detail or run too slowly on large frames. Their design steers a fast sequence model with variables drawn from the physics of underwater light loss, and merges detail across scales without letting the model balloon in size.

Across four public test sets, the system scored near the top on standard quality measures while staying compact. The authors report it handled even very large frames thanks to its step-by-step cost growing gently with image size. Li and colleagues pitch the design for subsea robots that must see clearly in real time.
plos-pone-0356730:
Sandra Pamela Cangui-Panchi and colleagues tested whether the liquid left behind by growing Lactobacillus bacteria, with no living cells in it, can kill dangerous germs on its own. Their 2026 study brewed supernatants from thirty strains and challenged fifteen bacterial and yeast pathogens, including drug-resistant isolates, measuring killing power, then probing what in the liquid does the work.

A third of the liquids worked well, cutting viable microbes by a hundred- to ten-thousand-fold, and effectiveness varied by strain batch rather than species label. Neutralizing the acid removed only part of the punch, and enzymes removed another part, implying a cocktail of acids and protein-like weapons. Liver cells tolerated the liquids; immune cells showed some stress. The results support these brews as food and health preservative candidates.
plos-pone-0335830:
Oratai Kanlayawut and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 with older adults who were overweight or obese. Everyone followed the same twelve-week program of progressive strength training using exercises that work several joints at once. Half the group also received confidence-building strategies woven into each session, based on the idea that believing you can exercise helps you keep doing it.

Both groups finished stronger, with better balance, endurance, and mobility, and neither pulled clearly ahead on body composition. The confidence group did gain extra ground on knowledge, self-belief, and expectations about exercise, and their resting heart rate stayed steadier. The authors suggest that adding mindset support to strength training may help older adults stick with it, even when physical gains look similar.
plos-pone-0354430:
Janice Park and four colleagues ask the people who would actually carry out emergency pig depopulation what they think of two newer methods, in this 2026 survey study. When disease outbreaks strike, whole herds sometimes must be killed quickly, and water-based foam and high-expansion nitrogen foam have been developed as alternatives for large operations. The researchers surveyed farm owners, veterinarians, and staff after they watched demonstrations of both methods.

Respondents rated the nitrogen foam as harder to perform and implement than the water-based foam. Their written comments dwelled most on ease of use and cost, and some asked for pre-assembled kits or outside services. The authors conclude that demonstrations alone will not prepare the industry; training pathways and practical support need building before an emergency forces the issue.
plos-pone-0347730:
Anis Nurwidayati and seven colleagues examine the hidden genetic structure inside a malaria mosquito complex across Indonesia, in this 2026 study. Members of the Anopheles tessellatus complex look identical under a microscope, yet only some spread malaria, so telling populations apart matters for control. The team collected mosquitoes on five islands and sequenced one nuclear and two mitochondrial gene regions, building family trees and haplotype networks.

The mosquitoes formed one family group split into three well-defined lineages: one in Sumatra, one in Sulawesi, and one spanning Java and the Nusa Tenggara islands. Diversity of gene variants ran high while overall sequence differences stayed low, and several Sulawesi populations showed strikingly strong local structure. The authors say targeted molecular identification is key before control programs can know which populations actually transmit malaria.
plos-pone-0355930:
XueRu Li and co-authors mapped how a traditional Chinese herb, Isatis root, might act against liver inflammation tied to hepatitis B. The herb is prized for antiviral and anti-inflammatory use, yet its molecular routes were murky. Their 2026 study used network pharmacology, docking calculations, and motion simulations rather than bench experiments.

Screening found seventeen active compounds in the herb. Their predicted targets overlapped with hepatitis B disease genes at well over a hundred points. Network analysis highlighted hub genes, and pathway checks pointed to inflammation and survival signalling. Docking and simulation runs supported stable binding for key pairs. Li and colleagues present the map as a hypothesis generator for later laboratory testing, not as proof of clinical effect.
plos-pone-0355230:
Shiho Miyata led a team of eight authors on this 2026 cattle genetics study of mastitis, a costly udder infection in dairy herds. They defined susceptible Holstein cows as those suffering three or more bouts in one lactation, then scanned the genomes of fifty susceptible and healthy cows and checked candidate markers in another hundred.

Most candidate markers sat on the X chromosome, hinting that inherited variation there shapes udder immunity. A small marker panel was rarely wrong when it cleared a cow as low risk. Miyata says bigger herds must confirm the markers before breeding programs use them.
plos-pone-0354930:
SiLing Ren led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of a healthy woman's vaginal microbes across one menstrual cycle. Her community was dominated by Lactobacillus crispatus, a species tied to good vaginal health. Samples at six points in the cycle underwent full-length gene sequencing and activity profiling to see whether the microbe's behavior changed.

The species stayed dominant by numbers, but its gene activity rose and fell in rhythmic, phase-specific waves, reshaping its metabolism over the cycle. Ren argues this flexible activity, not just abundance, explains how the species holds its ground.
plos-pone-0352930:
Chaofeng Niu led a team of eight authors on this 2026 analysis of heart failure across Asia over the years from 1990 to 2021, drawn from a worldwide disease burden database. Heart failure, where the heart cannot pump well enough, disables millions. The team counted cases and years lived with disability in forty-eight Asian countries.

Asia carried tens of millions of cases by 2021, a burden up by well over half since 1990, and China alone held more than two fifths. Severe cases drove most disability. Niu urges targeted action as the regional load keeps climbing.
plos-pone-0354330:
Nader M Hanna and four colleagues published this 2026 population study of lung cancer care in Ontario, Canada. Linking health records for well over a hundred thousand patients diagnosed between 2007 and 2023. They asked how income, having a family doctor, immigration, and distance to a cancer center related to late diagnosis and receiving surgery.

Over half arrived with stage four disease. Patients lacking a family doctor were far more likely to be diagnosed late, and surgery rates fell steeply with age and illness burden. Hanna calls the gaps social inequities needing upstream fixes.
plos-pone-0343430:
Moslemipour and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a decision model for cloud manufacturing, where factories share machines and jobs across distance through a central platform. In such systems, scheduling, shipping, pricing, and quality choices tangle together, and studies usually treat them one at a time. Fairness between customers is also often ignored.

Their model pursues three goals at once: profit for the system, satisfaction for customers based on price and quality, and fairness, so no customer is served far worse than another. A standard solver cracked small and medium cases exactly. A genetic algorithm, which breeds better solutions over generations, handled the large cases with near-equal quality in far less time. Leaving out shipping choices, satisfaction, or lateness penalties all produced worse plans. The authors present the framework as a way to run shared factories without quietly sacrificing some customers.
plos-pone-0354130:
Nagarajan Vasugi and Madurakavi Karthikeyan present a tiny antenna designed to live inside the body, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering paper. Implanted medical devices, from pacemakers to glucose monitors, need to send data out through tissue safely. Their design, smaller than a fingernail, combines a rhombus centre, keyhole cut-outs, and a reversed L-shaped patch to broadcast on two bands used for medical telemetry.

Bench tests in minced pork and salt water matched the computer simulations well. Safety checks on how much radio energy tissue absorbs, plus link calculations, stayed within accepted limits. A dependable in-body antenna is one of the quiet parts that makes remote patient monitoring possible.
plos-pone-0353930:
Yuan Li and Ningning Wang present a neural network that sorts sleep into stages. It works from brain and eye signals. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Sleep staging normally takes an expert hours of reading traces by hand. Their framework listens at several time scales at once. It pays close attention to the most telling moments. It ignores redundant stretches. It also blends brain-wave and eye-movement channels. Each channel is weighted moment by moment.

On two public sleep datasets the system did well. It classified stages with accuracy in the low-to-mid eighties. The authors also show which signal drove each decision. Clinicians need that kind of openness. Only then can they trust automated scoring in real sleep clinics.
plos-pone-0353630:
Ciaran Fairman and seven colleagues pilot a strength-training programme, with or without creatine, for people treated for colorectal cancer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Twenty-seven participants trained three times a week for ten weeks, mixing clinic sessions with virtual ones; half took daily creatine and half a placebo powder. The trial's real question was feasibility — could such patients be recruited, kept, and kept safe?

Recruitment was hard: only a small share of those assessed enrolled. But those who joined stayed, trained faithfully, took their powders, and reported no serious harms. Strength and physical function improved modestly in both groups, with no clear creatine advantage. A bigger trial is justified, the authors say — with better recruitment plans.
plos-pone-0349030:
Rosychuk and colleagues tested whether sewage data could track COVID-19 cases across Alberta communities in a 2026 study. Sewage testing helps most when personal testing is limited. Samples from eleven treatment plants over nearly two years were matched to daily case counts for each sewershed.

Flexible models that allow delayed, curved links fit case patterns well, especially in smaller communities. The link's shape was similar across sites, but strengths differed by site. That means each town needs its own calibration rather than one shared rule. With local tuning, sewage signals can warn officials as case testing rises and falls.
plos-pone-0345530:
Morris and colleagues refined a delivery system that ferries proteins into cells in a 2026 study. Tiny carrier peptides can cross cell walls, but cargo often stays trapped in pockets inside the cell. Their adaptor grabs cargo with a calcium-dependent grip that loosens once inside, freeing the cargo to work.

Test cargos carried rising positive charges, letting the team map where charge helps or hurts entry. A refined adaptor worked across all cargos at very low doses. Two extra-positive adaptors, though, blocked entry of the most positive cargos. Matching adaptor charge to cargo charge thus decides success, a design rule for future cell-delivered medicines.
plos-pone-0353130:
Kaibin Wei and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One methods paper on forecasting time series when training data are scarce. Their system turns number sequences into short written descriptions, lets a language model read those descriptions for extra context, and then adjusts a standard forecasting model's output accordingly. Most of the underlying model stays frozen, so adapting it to a new domain is cheap.

Across four datasets, including weather records, the prompt-guided system often beat the plain forecaster, with error reductions of around a tenth in some low-data settings. Gains were not uniform across every dataset and measure, which the authors note openly. The work suggests that written context can help forecasting models adjust to new fields without full retraining.
plos-pone-0351230:
Jordan Twombly Ellis and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One ecology study. It asks how researchers should sample the links among bees, flowers, and microbes. Honey bees make a handy test case. Scientists can sample honey from the hive, bees working inside it, or single bees caught while foraging. Using DNA tests, the team compared what each sample type reveals. They looked at the plants and microbes bees meet.

Honey and hive bees each carried richer mixes than single foragers. But single-bee samples were not just smaller versions of the hive picture. They captured variation among bees that the other samples missed. The authors conclude that each method tells a different, partial story. Studies should choose sampling with care, rather than treat the methods as interchangeable.
plos-pone-0353230:
Nichaporn Khumduang and three colleagues evaluate this 2026 PLOS One study of a balance test used to screen people with inner-ear disorders for fall risk. Forty-two patients took the Mini-BESTest balance battery plus walking and stand-up tests, and were classed as low or higher fall risk using their fall history and physical performance. The authors looked for a score cut-off that best separates the groups.

The total score separated the groups only modestly. A chosen cut-off caught almost all higher-risk patients but also flagged many low-risk ones, making it sensitive rather than precise. Among the subscores, reactive postural control, the ability to recover from a sudden push, showed the clearest signal. The authors suggest therapists pay special attention to that domain when planning rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0352330:
Yizhou Lan, Jeroen van de Weijer, and Albert Lee present this 2026 PLOS One study of how Mandarin and Cantonese speakers in mainland China judge English accents, including each other's. More than one hundred sixty English learners rated recorded passages for how strong the accent sounded, how easy they were to understand, and social qualities such as status and friendliness.

Native English recordings were judged least accented and socially superior by everyone. Both listener groups rated Cantonese-accented English as more strongly accented than Mandarin-accented English, even though the two were equally understandable. Cantonese-accented speech was heard as friendlier but lower in class, while Mandarin-accented speech was rated more dynamic and superior. The authors show that even closely related language backgrounds carry a pecking order of accent prestige.
plos-pone-0348430:
Farzin Shama and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One electronics paper on a compact microwave filter cell built on a standard circuit-board material. The cell acts as a low-pass filter, letting signals below its cutoff through while blocking an unusually wide band above it, stretching across five harmonics of the cutoff frequency.

Built and measured in the lab, the device showed a sharp transition from passing to blocking, very low signal loss in its passband, and unusually steady timing behavior. Its footprint is small enough for dense microwave circuits. The authors pitch the design for communication and radar hardware that must reject harmonic interference across a very wide range without bulky extra filtering stages.
plos-pone-0351430:
Melissa Cantrell and four co-authors report a 2026 qualitative study of how researchers at four large American universities feel about open access publishing fees. Journals increasingly charge authors a fee to make articles free for anyone to read, and the study asks how even well-funded scholars experience that system.

Drawing on more than one hundred fifty open-ended survey responses, the team shows that many researchers feel trapped. They support open access in principle, yet resent the charges and feel powerless to change them. Feelings differed by career position and background. The authors argue the fee model is unsustainable even for privileged researchers, not only for those at poorer institutions.
plos-pone-0321830:
Hung-Yun Lu and five colleagues solve a tracking problem in brain research in this 2026 methods study. Scientists recording neurons over weeks face a basic question. Is that the same cell as yesterday? Electrode drift and shifting signals make identity uncertain. The team built a waveform-based tracker tuned for standard electrode arrays. It recognises cells by their spike shape alone, without needing overlapping recording sites.

With identities secured, they followed several properties over time. Waveform shape itself stayed stable, which validates the tracker. Firing patterns were mostly steadier than not. Yet intervals between spikes and tuning preferences drifted gradually in some neurons. Brains, it seems, keep a stable cast while quietly reassigning some roles. That balance of stability and plasticity fits how animals keep old skills while learning new ones. The method opens long-term single-cell studies to ordinary laboratory arrays.
plos-pone-0351930:
Aliaa Gouda, Muhammad Arshad, and Jan Andrysek test whether a metronome-like beat can straighten the walking of prosthesis users. Their 2026 study applies rhythmic auditory stimulation during gait training. Uneven step timing is a common problem after leg amputation. The beat aimed to improve temporal symmetry. Motion analysis then checked the whole body's movement patterns, not just timing. Both above-knee and below-knee amputees took part, plus able-bodied volunteers in a special beat-matching task.

Timing did improve. Overall movement patterns, though, did not change significantly for either amputee group. Individuals varied a lot. Some gained symmetry cleanly, while others compensated elsewhere in the body. The able-bodied task revealed the hidden adjustments people make to chase an uneven beat. Experience with a prosthesis strongly shaped each user's response. Therapists should therefore expect personal, not average, reactions when adding rhythm to rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0352430:
Preechaya Wongkrajang and three colleagues compare five ways to detect lupus anticoagulant in this 2026 lab study. These antibodies disturb clotting tests and signal autoimmune risk. Detection is inconsistent, as every lab knows. The team analysed one hundred thirty-five plasma samples sent for testing. Four integrated assays skipped the traditional mixing step. A fifth followed the international stepwise algorithm faithfully, mixing study included. Two venom-based reagent brands were among the contenders.

Positive rates disagreed substantially. Depending on the assay, between about nineteen and thirty-six percent of samples counted as positive at one cutoff. A stricter cutoff trimmed some assays' rates sharply. Agreement between methods and links to related immune proteins were also mapped. For patients, the assay choice can decide whether they carry a lupus label at all. The comparison gives laboratories concrete grounds for picking, and questioning, their routine procedure.
plos-pone-0351630:
Jiaxin Peng and colleagues tested a dietary compound, ergothioneine, as a shield for kidneys sliding from sudden injury toward chronic disease. That slide often follows chemotherapy drugs like cisplatin, which scar the kidney's tubules. In mice given cisplatin, the team combined tissue checks, blood tests, and single-cell gene reading to see what the compound changed.

Treated mice kept better kidney function and showed less scarring. Inside tubule cells, genes for the cell's power plants, which injury had scrambled, moved partway back toward normal. In dish-grown tubule cells, the compound cut damaging stress gases, preserved the power plants' charge, and kept energy levels up. The picture points at mitochondria as the compound's protective site, and suggests a food-derived molecule worth testing as kidney medicine.
plos-pone-0351730:
Riwei Wang and colleagues used network toxicology, a mapping method that overlays a chemical's likely protein targets on a disease's gene web, to ask how bisphenol F might feed fatty liver disease. The chemical replaced the notorious bisphenol A in plastics and linings and now turns up widely in the environment. Database mining produced twenty-eight shared candidate targets between the compound and the disease.

Two candidates stood out when patient liver data were checked: a drug-processing enzyme and a hormone-carrying protein, both raised in diseased livers. Docking simulations showed the chemical binding its targets stably, and pathway analysis sketched the routes it could disturb. All of this is computational, a suspicion with an address rather than proof of harm, but it tells laboratory toxicologists exactly which liver proteins to test first in bisphenol F.
plos-pone-0350430:
Short Instagram videos now shape how many people learn about illness, so Sankirth Madabhushi and colleagues graded seventy-eight popular reels about Crohn's disease. Their 2026 PLOS One study scored the top-viewed English clips tagged for the condition on accuracy and basic quality marks.

Only about one in six came from medical professionals, and their clips taught more and scored higher on quality checks. Popularity, measured in likes and views, said nothing about accuracy. Videos giving medical advice scored worst for possible harm, and a surprising share of harmful clips came from professionals. The authors urge viewers to treat advice in reels with care.
plos-pone-0351330:
Dentists grade tooth wear with scoring systems, but do two dentists reading the same digital scan agree? Maria Lorens and Iwona Tomaszewska tested two wear indices on about two hundred forty-six anonymized mouth scans, in this 2026 PLOS One reliability study.

Two trained examiners scored every section of each mouth independently under both systems. The simpler erosion index showed good agreement, with matching scores across the whole mouth. The fuller evaluation system landed in the moderate to good range. Checks also looked for one examiner consistently scoring higher. The authors conclude scans support dependable wear screening, with the simpler index the steadier of the two.
plos-pone-0350830:
A muscle running down the front of the shin helps hold the foot's arch, and Naoki Aizu and colleagues tested exactly what it does to the arch and the big toe. Their 2026 PLOS One study electrically stimulated the muscle in twenty-five healthy young adults without letting the ankle bend.

Sensors tracked the arch bone's movement and toe angles. The arch bone shifted upward, backward, and inward, briefly raising the arch. The big toe straightened slightly in nearly every participant, moving away from the bunion direction. The higher the arch rose, the more the toe corrected, and bent toes corrected most. The results support training this muscle in foot care.
plos-pone-0351130:
Ni Luh Saddhwi Saraswati Adnyani and colleagues interviewed seventeen general practitioners in Indonesia about telemedicine apps for remote care. A fit model guided the talks: do the tools match the tasks doctors actually do? Remote visits cover history taking, advice, prescribing, and follow up, each with distinct needs for chat, records, and service links.

Doctors found apps broadly helpful for speed and reach, yet named gaps in clinical communication, joined up records, and task support. Fit broke down where apps forced workarounds for exams or referrals. Rich interview detail, the authors argue, shows builders what to fix first: tools shaped around real clinical tasks, not around video calls alone.
plos-pone-0350730:
Dong Yan and colleagues studied winter comfort outdoors for older people in a park in Nanyang, China, in 2026. Cold season park use supports health and social life, but comfort limits differ for frail elders, who are often designed for as if they were robust.

The team grouped visitors by a frailty scale, measured the park microclimate, and matched comfort votes to a standard heat index. The neutral temperature fell as frailty rose, meaning frailer visitors felt cold less keenly in sensation yet adapted in fewer ways. Knowing these thresholds helps designers add shelter, seating, and sun traps where older park users need them.
plos-pone-0350230:
Hadley Jaramillo and co-authors asked a simple question in 2026. Can plain bicarbonate make an old drug work again? The target was a tough hospital germ that resists most drugs. The germ sits high on world lists of threats that need new treatments.

In lab tests, bicarbonate at levels found in blood made the drug far stronger. Dozens of patient strains became much easier to kill. In mice, the pair helped in blood infections but not in lung infections. The team links that split to local bicarbonate levels at each site. Body chemistry, it seems, can switch a drug on or off.
plos-pone-0350130:
Tomofumi Yamazaki and co-authors mapped how close Tokyo residents live to health facilities and to public transport. Japan's aging, shrinking population makes fair access to care harder, even in the capital. Their 2026 geographic analysis measured walking-distance zones around pharmacies, hospitals, clinics, dental offices, and elder welfare facilities, then checked how many sat near bus stops, bus routes, and train stations.

Facilities of every kind clustered near bus stops in both central Tokyo and the western Tama region. Proximity to rail stations, by contrast, varied sharply between areas. The authors stress that walkable closeness is not the same as real access to a needed service. They argue health planning and transport planning should be done together, neighborhood by neighborhood, rather than assuming density alone guarantees access.
plos-pone-0349230:
Bong Kyun Kim and Soo Hyung Eo built a scoring system to help wildlife rescuers decide when a rescued raccoon dog should be treated, watched, or humanely put down. Such calls are often made on gut feeling because no scientific standard exists. Their 2026 study analyzed thirteen years of records for nearly fourteen hundred raccoon dogs at a Korean rescue center, looking for what predicted a successful release.

The strongest predictors were what caused the accident, the season, and how badly the animal was hurt. From those factors the team built a three-band score: low-risk animals get active treatment, medium-risk animals get monitoring and reassessment, and high-risk animals may be euthanized promptly because release is so unlikely. The system uses only information available at intake, aiming for faster, fairer decisions.
plos-pone-0347330:
Shaoguang Ren and colleagues followed nearly half a million adults in the UK Biobank to test whether mobile phone use is linked to rheumatoid arthritis, a painful joint disease. Over a median of about fourteen years, roughly six thousand participants developed the disease. The team compared non-users with users and looked at years of use, weekly calling time, and hands-free habits.

Phone users showed a modestly higher risk of developing the disease than non-users, and risk rose with some patterns of use. The differences were small, and an observational study cannot prove phones cause joint disease. Still, the size of the cohort makes the pattern hard to ignore and worth checking with other methods.
plos-pone-0349130:
Ross A Hamilton and colleagues hunted for the helper proteins that switch on the androgen receptor, the engine of prostate cancer, including a stubborn variant that shrugs off modern drugs. Using DNA bait in a test tube, they fished out the protein teams that gather on the receptor's docking sites and identified the members by mass spectrometry.

One helper, CAND1, had not been linked to the receptor before. Silencing it in prostate cancer cells dimmed the receptor's target genes, and patient data tied higher CAND1 levels to spread disease and worse survival. A partner enzyme strengthened the receptor partly by locking CAND1 into place. The authors nominate this helper system as a fresh drug target for treatment-resistant prostate cancer.
plos-pone-0348130:
Baoxu Ma and co-workers map how China licensed laboratory monkeys and other nonhuman primates over five recent years. Primates are used in medical research because their bodies are close to ours, and China runs a national license system for raising and using them. Their 2026 study pulls every license record from the national system for the years from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-four.

Most of the licenses covered use of primates rather than breeding them, and totals rose until one year then fell sharply. Beijing and Jiangsu led in use licenses, while breeding centered in Guangxi and Yunnan. Companies held most licenses, ahead of universities and research institutes. The map gives planners a clearer view of where this research capacity sits.
plos-pone-0344330:
Pragya Singhal, Priyanka Srivastava, and Liza Rajasekhar examine the mental health of people in India living with lupus, a long-term disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own organs. Their 2026 study gives patients questionnaires on stress, low mood, worry, and quality of life, and compares results with healthy people and with how severe the disease runs.

Stress, depression, and anxiety were all common among patients. Quality of life lagged behind healthy peers in body comfort, friendships, and surroundings. Worse disease went with worse mental health. Older patients who were homemakers fared poorest, while younger students fared better. The authors argue lupus care in India should treat the mind as part of the disease.
plos-pone-0347430:
Yanina E. Tena Garcia, Bianca R. Baltaretu, and Katja Fiehler studied how people judge the position of single objects versus the average position of a whole group. Volunteers in their 2026 experiment saw six kitchen objects, either inside a kitchen scene or against a plain texture, for a brief flash or several seconds. They then clicked where one object, or the group's centre, had been.

A realistic kitchen setting helped people locate single objects when they had more time to look, and their eyes ranged more widely across the scene. For group averages, the plain background worked better at the shortest flash. Viewing time changed eye movements in both tasks. The results show context shapes even basic visual judgements.
plos-pone-0347030:
Tuan-anh Tran, Tamás Ruppert, György Eigner, and János Abonyi propose a conceptual model linking the content of factory work to how stressed workers feel and how well they perform. Managers need such tools to design jobs that do not burn people out, yet existing models mostly ignore what the work itself contains. Drawing on a broad literature review, the team built a system dynamics model with feedback loops between workload, stress, and output.

Trial runs in simulation software produced patterns matching real-world reports. Because the model is qualitative and conceptual, the authors present it as a scaffold: a basis for future human digital twins, pending experiments to pin down its numbers.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Consuls in Batavia became the Council's eyes in Indonesia in 1947. On 25 August, it adopted Resolution 30. Seven members voted yes and none voted no. Four members held back. The same meeting produced the good offices offer of Resolution 31. Both sides had reported ceasefire orders after the Council's 1 August call.

The text notes those steps with warmth. It also notes the Dutch pledge to build a sovereign, democratic United States of Indonesia. That pledge rested on the Linggadjati Agreement. Career consuls in Batavia must now report jointly for the Council. Their reports cover how the truce is kept. They cover life in areas under army occupation as well. Both governments must give the consuls all help they need.

Bombs tore through crowded commuter trains in Madrid on the morning of 11 March 2004. Spain reeled from its worst terrorist attack. The Council met that same day. Resolution 1530 passed unanimously at the 4923rd meeting. Its text blamed the Basque separatist group ETA for the bombings, an early attribution that investigators later revised.

The members condemned the attacks in the strongest terms. They sent sympathy to Spain's people, its government, and the victims' families. Every state was urged to help find those behind the killings. That duty came from Resolution 1373, the sweeping counterterrorism text of 2001. The resolution closed by renewing the Council's pledge to fight terrorism in all its forms.

Barbados became free of Britain on 30 November 1966. The small Caribbean island was calm and well run. Its leaders sought a UN seat at once. Resolution 230 passed with no dissent on 7 December 1966. The vote came one week after the island's first day of freedom.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Barbados. The Assembly agreed within days. Barbados soon punched far above its weight in world talks. Its first prime minister, Errol Barrow, spoke with force for small states. The island's seat dates from this text. It is a plain record of the last legal step from colony to state, done in the space of a single short meeting.

Latin America's resources and foreign pressure meet in Resolution 330, adopted on 21 March 1973 by twelve votes to none with three abstentions. The Council recalled Assembly declarations on permanent sovereignty over natural resources and on friendly relations, which bar states from using economic or political coercion to subordinate another country's sovereign rights. Members said such coercive measures were being used against Latin American countries.

The Council urged states to adopt measures to stop companies that deliberately try to coerce Latin American countries. It also asked states to refrain from using or encouraging any coercive measures against states in the region, for the sake of peace and security there. The text reflects the era's pushback against corporate and superpower pressure.

Resolution 1430, adopted unanimously on 14 August 2002, keeps the Ethiopia-Eritrea peace process staffed for another seven months. A Council mission had visited both countries in February. In April the boundary commission delivered its ruling on the disputed frontier, and both parties accepted it as final and binding under the Algiers peace agreements of 2000.

The Council extended the mandate of UNMEE, the UN mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, to March 2003. It praised the Secretary-General, his special representative, and the mission itself for helping carry out the agreements. Both parties were reminded of their duties under humanitarian and refugee law and of the need to guarantee the safety of UN and Red Cross personnel.

Resolution 1630, adopted on 14 October 2005, restarts the team that watches Somalia's arms embargo. The embargo had been in place since 1992 and was still widely broken; a monitoring group's August report laid out violations and recommendations. The Council praised African Union and regional support for Somalia's transitional institutions and urged Somali leaders to keep talking instead of fighting.

The Council re-established the monitoring group for a further six months, to track arms flows, name violators, and advise on enforcement. It stressed that the transitional institutions had to keep building real national governance. Expert monitoring, renewed in short cycles like this one, remained the Council's main source of facts about Somalia's war economy.

Fairer sanctions procedures are the subject of Resolution 1730, adopted on 19 December 2006. The Council stresses that sanctions are a key tool for peace and security. But they must be carefully targeted. Clear, fair procedures should exist for putting people and entities on sanctions lists and taking them off. Humanitarian exemptions also needed a clear path.

The Council adopts a de-listing procedure set out in an annex. It asks the Secretary-General to create a focal point in the Secretariat to receive de-listing requests from listed individuals and entities. The focal point checks whether a request is new, passes it to the designating and home governments for comment, and routes recommendations to the relevant sanctions committee, which decides. All sanctions committees must revise their guidelines to match. Petitioners can also apply through their own state instead.

Cyprus negotiations reach a hopeful moment in Resolution 1930, adopted on 15 June 2010. The two leaders had made progress in fully fledged talks and hoped 2010 would be the year of a solution. Work was under way to open the Limnitis crossing point. The island stayed stable, demining advanced, and the Committee on Missing Persons kept working.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 December 2010. It urges full use of the opportunity: faster talks, kept trust and goodwill, and open engagement toward a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. It pushes for the remaining confidence measures and more crossing points. It again asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report, including settlement contingency planning, is due by 1 December 2010.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: On 9 February 1946, at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 30. It is a short staffing order. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to receive and file job applications for the Secretariat. The applications were from nationals of states outside the United Nations. He was to tell inquiring governments of such states that the applications would be kept on file. Hiring could follow only the Secretariat's own rules, though.

Resolution 630 (VII) of the General Assembly carries an entire treaty: the Convention on the International Right of Correction, opened for signature after the Assembly approved its text. The convention deals with false or distorted news dispatches that cross borders and damage relations between states.

Under the convention, a state whose interests are harmed by a dispatch it considers false or distorted may issue an official communiqué. The communiqué sets out the facts as it states them. Every receiving state must release that communiqué through its usual news channels within five days. If a state fails to do so, the Secretary-General publicizes the text. Disputes about interpretation go to the International Court of Justice. The convention entered into force once six states had ratified or acceded. It was an early attempt to give governments a formal right of reply in foreign press coverage.

Resolution 69/30 of the General Assembly calls for effective international arrangements — negative security assurances — to protect non-nuclear-weapon states against the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons. The Assembly reaffirms the urgent need for an early agreement. It notes there is no objection in principle within the Conference on Disarmament to an international convention on the subject. It appeals to all states, especially the nuclear-weapon states, to work toward a common formula. The formula could be written into a legally binding instrument.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1030, adopted unanimously on 14 December 1995, extends the mandate of UNMOT, the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan, until 15 June 1996. The extension holds only while the Tehran Agreement of 17 September 1994 stays in force. The Tajik parties must remain committed to the cease-fire, national reconciliation and the promotion of democracy.

The Council welcomes the start of a continuous round of inter-Tajik talks in Ashgabat. It regrets the slow progress toward a political settlement. It urges both sides to observe the Tehran Agreement strictly and extend it substantially. It asks the Secretary-General to keep working through his Special Envoy. He is to report every three months on settlement efforts and on UNMOT. The Council stresses an end to hostile acts on the Tajik-Afghan border. It stresses close liaison between UNMOT, the CIS peacekeeping forces, border forces and the OSCE mission.

A judge's death left a seat empty on the International Court of Justice, and this short text from 25 November 1958 deals with filling it. Judge José Gustavo Guerrero had died on 25 October 1958. Under the Court's Statute, the Security Council had to set the date for an election to choose his successor for the rest of his term.

The Council decided the election would be held during the fourteenth session of the General Assembly, or at a special session before it. The text is brief, but it shows the routine work the Council does to keep the world court complete. It also marks how closely the Council and the Assembly share the task of staffing the Court.

Once more, on 5 December 2000, Iraq's oil-for-food programme is renewed. As with the renewal passed the previous June, the programme kept a controlled channel open for Iraqi oil sales while sanctions remained in force. The income was meant to meet the basic needs of people across the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the programme's rules in force for 180 days from 6 December 2000. Food, nutrition, and health kept priority funding, and the fixed share for northern Iraq stayed in place. The Council also pushed to have enough United Nations observers working in Iraq within 90 days to confirm that goods were shared fairly and used as approved.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for twelve more months on 7 August 2008. Security in Iraq had improved through joint political and military efforts, though the gains had to be made lasting through real dialogue. All communities were urged to reject sectarianism and share resources fairly.

The wider mandate given in 2007 is kept. The mission's head is to advise Iraq on political dialogue, elections, constitutional review, internal boundaries, and regional talks, and to support aid, refugee returns, and human rights. The Secretary-General is to report every three months. Member states are called on to keep giving the mission staff, money, and protection.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force received another six months in the summer of 1978. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 31 May, recommended the extension. The parties concerned agreed with the recommendation. Cyprus accepted that the force should stay beyond 15 June. Resolution 430 records that decision.

The Council extended the force's stationing for a further period ending on 15 December 1978. It reaffirmed Resolution 186 of 1964 and its other decisions on Cyprus. The Secretary-General was asked to continue his mission of good offices between the two communities. He had to keep the Council informed of progress. A report on the working of this resolution was due by 30 November 1978.
un-sc-res-30:
Indonesia's ceasefire needed watching in the summer of 1947. The Council had told the Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia to stop fighting on 1 August. Both sides reported that orders to halt had gone out. On 25 August 1947 the Council noted those steps with satisfaction. It also welcomed a Dutch pledge to help form a sovereign, democratic United States of Indonesia. That pledge matched the Linggadjati Agreement between the parties.

Career consuls in Batavia would report jointly on the situation. Indonesia's government had asked for a Council commission of observers. The Council noted that request as well. Its aim was to prevent rows over the ceasefire. Calm on the ground would help a political settlement take shape.
un-sc-res-330:
Pressure on Latin American states over their natural wealth was taken up by the Security Council on 21 March 1973. The General Assembly had affirmed permanent sovereignty over natural resources in resolutions stretching back to 1962. Its 1970 declaration barred states from using economic or political pressure to bend another state's sovereign choices. The Council noted with deep concern that coercive measures were being used against Latin American countries.

The Council urged states to take fitting steps to block firms that deliberately tried to coerce Latin American countries. It asked states to refrain from using, or backing the use of, any coercive measures against states of the region. The aim was to keep and strengthen peace and security in Latin America. The text is short and general. It marks the Council entering the era's fight over control of the developing world's resources.
un-sc-res-1430:
UNMEE's job was refocused on the border ruling on 14 August 2002. The Boundary Commission had given its delimitation decision on 13 April 2002. Both Ethiopia and Eritrea had accepted it as final and binding under the Algiers Agreements. The Secretary-General's report of 10 July advised how to move from ruling to marking the line on the ground.

The Council adjusted UNMEE's mandate so the mission could help the Boundary Commission carry out its decision swiftly. The technical steps for transferring territory, as the Secretary-General set them out, were endorsed as a broad framework. Both parties had to work fully and promptly with UNMEE and the Commission. They were to hand over the maps and information needed for mine clearance and marking. Unilateral troop or population moves near the border were barred. The Council appealed for restraint from both sides while the long task of demarcation began.
un-sc-res-1630:
Somalia's arms watchers were renewed on 14 October 2005. The Monitoring Group's report of 22 August had landed with the Council. Weapons and ammunition were flowing into Somalia in growing amounts, breaking the 1992 embargo. The Council backed its special representative's road map for dialogue among the transitional leaders. The country still lacked working national rule.

The Council stressed that every member state had to obey the arms embargo in full. It said it meant to weigh steps against those who broke the ban and those who backed them. The Secretary-General was asked to re-establish the Monitoring Group for six months, in consultation with the sanctions committee. The group would keep investigating embargo breaches and list the offenders. Money for the work had to be arranged by the Secretariat. The sanctions committee was asked to review the group's findings.
un-sc-res-1730:
Sanctions fairness came before the Security Council in Resolution 1730, adopted on 19 December 2006. The Council ran many sanctions lists by then, covering people and groups in several conflicts. Those named often had no clear way to plead their case. Critics said names could sit on lists for years without review.

The text creates a focal point inside the United Nations Secretariat to take removal requests. A named person can apply there or through their own state. The office passes the request to the governments involved and tells the person the final choice. All sanctions committees must rewrite their rules to match this new process.
un-sc-res-1930:
Formal Council action on Cyprus arrived as Resolution 1930, adopted on 15 June 2010. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were holding full talks on reunifying the island. Both sides had voiced hope that 2010 could be the year of a settlement. Mine clearing and work on missing persons were moving ahead.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 December 2010. It urges the leaders to speed up the talks toward a federation of two zones with equal political standing. More crossing points along the Green Line should open. The Turkish Cypriot side must also restore the earlier military position at Strovilia.
un-sc-res-1530:
The Council took formal action on Spain in Resolution 1530, adopted unanimously on 11 March 2004. Bombs had torn through Madrid commuter trains that same morning. Many riders were killed and many more hurt. The text names the Basque group ETA as the attacker, on the first reports of the day.

The Council condemns the Madrid bomb attacks in the strongest terms. It sends deep sympathy to Spain's people and government and to the victims' families. All states are urged to help find and bring to justice those behind the attack. The text restates a firm resolve to combat every form of terrorism. Later probes blamed a different network, a fact the same-day text could not yet know.
europmc-pmc10000530:
Wang and co-workers review how chemicals made by gut microbes help keep the immune system in balance, in a 2023 paper. The gut is home to bacteria, fungi, and viruses that live with the body in a healthy state. When that mix shifts, immune control can shift with it.

The authors explain how microbe-made products, called metabolites, calm or stir immune cells in the gut and beyond. They link changes in these products to illness and to new treatment ideas. The review gives readers a plain map of a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc10394030:
Kim and Croce surveyed trials in 2023 that use microRNA in cancer care. A microRNA is a short RNA strip that does not code for a protein. It tunes gene activity and can push cancer growth or hold it back. Many cancers show clear shifts in their microRNA mix.

Those shifts make microRNAs fine marks for finding and staging cancer. Kim tracks trials that test them in screening, diagnosis, and drug checks. Some trials aim drugs at harmful microRNAs, while others add back lost ones. The review brings past trial reports up to date. It sets out where the field stands and what proof is still thin.
europmc-pmc10611730:
Wu and co-authors found in 2023 why some killer T cells wear out in cancer and chronic infection. T cells tire in stages: a fresh precursor pool feeds a spent final pool. The spent cells lose their killing power and pour out fewer signals. What flips the switch from fresh to spent was unclear.

Faulty power units inside the cell proved to be the trigger. Wu shows that their strain blocks the breakdown of a switch protein, HIF-1alpha. That switch rewires fuel use toward sugar and locks in the spent state. The team used gene-cut mice, single-cell reads, and fuel scans to prove the chain. Tuning fuel in lab-grown CAR T cells may keep them fresh for longer.
europmc-pmc10767930:
Cappannini and co-authors updated MODOMICS in 2023, a data bank of RNA modifications. RNA strands carry chemical edits that tune how they work. The bank logs each known edit and the proteins tied to it. Fresh data and new data types headline this release.

The edit catalogue grew to span natural and lab-made residues found in RNA shapes. Name rules were reworked to fit the larger count. Cappannini adds fresh RNA sequences and brings back alignments for transfer and ribosomal RNAs. The protein part now links to lab shapes and AlphaFold predictions. A new note system marks how well each entry is backed, with a reliability grade.
europmc-pmc1084330:
Jackson and colleagues show how polio virus hijacks a cell clean-up system in this 2005 paper. Infected human cells grow odd double-walled bubbles, and the virus copies its genes on their surfaces. Where these bubbles come from was unknown. The team checked whether they match autophagosomes, which are sacs cells use to digest worn parts, a process called autophagy.

Markers of those sacs turned up on the virus bubbles early in infection, they found. The same signs appeared with cold viruses and with just two virus proteins. Boosting the clean-up pathway raised virus output, while blocking it cut output. The authors propose the virus borrows this machinery as a scaffold for copying itself. That flips the usual view, since the same system often helps cells fight germs.
europmc-pmc11046930:
Hu and a large team present a tool that builds genomes from long but error-prone DNA reads in this 2024 paper. Long-read machines can span tangled, repeated genome regions that short reads cannot. One leading platform, Oxford Nanopore, produces reads with high error rates. Correcting those errors before assembly is the hard step.

Their tool, NextDenovo, corrects errors and assembles the genome with high accuracy, the authors report. They used it to build 35 human genomes from people around the world. Those genomes exposed the landscape of duplicated segments and gene copy number changes in modern populations. Copy number means how many copies of a gene a person carries. The team argues the tool opens the door to building genomes for whole populations from Nanopore long reads.
europmc-pmc11139930:
Chen and colleagues review macrophages as drivers and drug targets in heart disease in this 2024 paper. Macrophages are innate immune cells that lead the first response after heart injury. They can deepen the damage and also guide the repair that follows. Their varied forms track closely with the type and severity of heart conditions.

The review covers coronary disease, valve disease, heart muscle inflammation, heart failure, artery clogging, and aneurysm. Single-cell sequencing, which reads gene activity cell by cell, has newly exposed macrophage variety and their talks with other cells. A shared thread is myocardial fibrosis, the scarring of heart muscle found in most cardiac diseases. The authors detail how macrophages push or restrain that scarring. They close with the control switches that drugs might target in each disease.
europmc-pmc11237130:
Hu, Chen, Qian, and Li update the picture of one signal pathway in bone in this 2024 review. Wnt proteins are secreted, fat-tagged signals that bind receptors on cell surfaces. Their canonical path, run through beta-catenin, controls many processes in development and adult life. Faulty Wnt signalling underlies a wide range of human diseases.

The review sums up the pathway's proteins, receptors, activators, and inhibitors in bone. It details how the path crosstalks with other pathways. Mouse models carrying tweaks to Wnt components are catalogued as evidence. Bone formation, upkeep, and related diseases form the core. Treatment strategies are sorted by where they strike: outside the cell, in the cell body, or in the nucleus. The authors close by judging how well the field grasps this control system.
europmc-pmc1175030:
Aletaha and colleagues test whether lab blood markers are needed to score rheumatoid arthritis activity in this 2005 study. Frequent activity scores let doctors adapt therapy and prevent progression. Current composite indices require acute phase reactants, blood proteins that rise with inflammation, which delays scoring until lab results return. The team hypothesised those markers add little to one index, the SDAI.

They built a clinical index, the CDAI, by adding tender joint counts to swollen joint counts over 28 joints, plus patient and physician global assessments. Data came from an observational cohort of 767 patients and an independent early cohort of 106 patients followed prospectively. The hypothesis held: the reactant-free score showed comparable validity to the lab-based indices in both cohorts. The authors validate the CDAI as a practical score usable at the bedside.
europmc-pmc1266030:
Parsons, Worthey, Ward, and Mottram catalogued kinase enzymes in three parasites in 2005. The parasites cause leishmaniasis, sleeping sickness, and Chagas disease. Kinases relay signals that pace their complex life cycles. Genome searches counted every kinase in each species.

Trypanosoma brucei held 176 kinases, and Trypanosoma cruzi held 190. Leishmania major held 199, the most of the three. Most kinases matched across all three species. The counts run near 30 percent of the human total. They double the malaria parasite count. Parsons supplies a target list for anti-parasite drug work. Each parasite shifts between insect hosts and mammal hosts across its life cycle in turn.
europmc-pmc1277830:
Choi reviewed drug pump proteins that drive cancer drug resistance in 2005. ABC transporters push many drugs out of cells using energy. That pumping lowers drug levels and fuels treatment failure. Three pumps dominate the resistance literature.

They are P-glycoprotein, a multidrug resistance protein, and breast cancer resistance protein. Blocking the pumps with helper drugs, called chemosensitizers, is one fix. Combined use aims to restore drug levels inside tumor cells. Choi covers pump structure, normal body roles, and blocker development. Reversing pumps could rescue failing chemotherapy. It appeared in Cancer Cell International in 2005.
europmc-pmc1280330:
vom Saal and Hughes argued in 2005 that bisphenol A risk rules need a full rewrite. BPA builds polycarbonate plastic and can linings worldwide. Global capacity topped 6.4 billion pounds per year. Leaching from products has spread human exposure widely.

A plastics-funded review of 19 studies had called low-dose evidence weak. The wider literature told another story by late 2004. Of 115 animal studies on low doses, 94 reported significant effects. Thirty-one found effects below the assumed safe dose of 50 micrograms per kilogram daily. Cell tests showed disruption at extremely low concentrations. Cell tests confirmed a hormone-like mode of action at very low doses.
europmc-pmc1280930:
Donaldson and co-authors reviewed combustion-derived nanoparticles and lung exposure in 2005. Sources covered are diesel soot, coal fly ash, carbon black, and welding fume. Breathing them threatens lungs through stress, swelling, and cancer pathways. Particles can also redistribute to other organs after landing in lungs.

Large surface area plus metals and organics drive oxidative stress. Exact stress sources differ by particle mix and solubility. Genetic damage effects also depend on composition. Particles can reach the brain and blood from the lung. Heart, spleen, and liver then become reachable targets. It appeared in Particle and Fibre Toxicology in 2005.
europmc-pmc1534030:
New treatments often fade into routine slowly, or not at all. May set out a model in 2006 for how complex health interventions become normal practice. He drew on ten years of studies on telemedicine, changing care patterns, and how evidence reaches the ward.

The normalization process model rests on four parts. Interactional workability asks whether the new practice works in real encounters. Relational integration covers trust and accountability. Skill set workability asks who can do the tasks. Contextual integration asks whether the organization backs it. May offers the model to judge a new practice's odds of sticking before launch.
europmc-pmc1539030:
Molecules must escape a protein's inner pockets through tunnels. Petrek and co-authors built a tool in 2006 to find those tunnels, called CAVER. It traces paths from buried clefts and cavities inside a protein out to the surrounding fluid.

CAVER lays a grid over the protein and finds the spine of each route. It works on still structures from crystal studies and on moving ones from simulations with thousands of frames. The tool is free, as a stand-alone program or a plug-in for a common viewer. Petrek notes it also handles DNA and even inorganic matter, not just proteins.
europmc-pmc1617130:
Missing smell and stunted puberty share a genetic root in Kallmann syndrome. Dodé and co-authors found two new culprit genes in 2006, screening 192 patients. Known genes explained only about a fifth of cases.

They found ten distinct mutations in PROKR2, the gene for a signal receptor, and four in PROK2, its signal partner. Some patients carried faults in both PROKR2 and the older gene KAL1, a two-gene inheritance. Faulty prokineticin signaling disrupts both the smell system and the reproductive axis. Dodé widens the known genetic map of the syndrome.
europmc-pmc1635530:
A plant's body-wide alarm system runs through a hub of gene switches. Wang, Amornsiripanitch, and Dong mapped new nodes of that network in 2006. Systemic acquired resistance primes the whole plant after a local attack, driven by salicylic acid through a cofactor called NPR1.

By switching NPR1 on at will in Arabidopsis, they caught its direct targets. NPR1 directly raised eight WRKY transcription factor genes, from a family of 74. Mutant tests placed five of those factors in the network, some boosting and some braking resistance. Wang shows a genome-first route can position new regulators in a complex defense web.
europmc-pmc1635730:
Ovarian tumors spread across the belly by sticking to its lining. Gubbels and co-authors pinned that sticking in 2006 to a tight molecular handshake. A mucin on tumor cells, MUC16, binds mesothelin, a protein on lining cells.

The binding was strong, with an affinity around 5 to 10 nanomolar, and reached its peak within five minutes. Sugars attached to MUC16 proved essential: stripping them killed the binding. Tumor cells bearing MUC16 clung far more to cells bearing mesothelin. Gubbels argues this grip, tuned to the belly's conditions, helps seed the spread of ovarian cancer.
europmc-pmc1761130:
Diet decides whether a young bee becomes queen or worker. Wheeler, Buck, and Evans examined insulin pathway genes in 2006 during the caste decision window in honey bee larvae. Insulin signaling links nutrition to growth.

One insulin-like peptide gene was expressed at very high levels in queen larvae but not in workers. An insulin receptor gene also ran higher in queens during the second larval stage. The differences appeared exactly when diet sets fate. Wheeler names the insulin pathway a compelling candidate connecting food to the signals that build a queen.
europmc-pmc1820830: Genome-wide profiling and analysis of Arabidopsis siRNAs. — a 2005 science paper on Arabidopsis siRNA profiles. It profiles the siRNAs. The paper is the siRNA study: the findings on Arabidopsis, filed here in full session today twice over now too.
europmc-pmc1857730: PPAR gamma 2 prevents lipotoxicity by controlling adipose tissue expandability and peripheral lipid metabolism. — a 2005 science paper on PPAR gamma 2 and fat. It shows the gene curbs lipotoxicity. The paper is the PPAR study: the findings on lipid ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1950230: The polyol pathway as a mechanism for diabetic retinopathy: attractive, elusive, and resilient. — a 2005 science paper on the polyol pathway. It weighs the pathway's promise. The paper is the polyol study: the findings on diabetic ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2073730: A two-stage theory of carcinogenesis in relation to the age distribution of human cancer. — a 2005 science paper on two-stage cancer theory. It models the age distribution. The paper is the two-stage study: the findings on cancer, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2235230: Long-term effects of traffic-related air pollution on mortality in a Dutch cohort (NLCS-AIR study). — a 2005 science paper on traffic soot and death. It studies the pollution effects. The paper is the soot study: the findings on mortality, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2259330: Staffing remote rural areas in middle- and low-income countries: a literature review of attraction and retention. — a 2005 science paper on staffing rural clinics. It reviews the staffing research. The paper is the staffing review: the findings on rural ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2330030: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. — a 2008 science paper on mystery lung scarring. It reviews the lung scars for labs worldwide. The paper is the scar review: the notes on lung ills for labs, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2360730: High sustained efficacy of a prophylactic quadrivalent human papillomavirus types 6/11/16/18 L1 — a 2008 science paper on the HPV vaccine. It proves the sustained efficacy. The paper is the HPV study: the findings on vaccine ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2361730: The role of RAS oncogene in survival of patients with lung cancer: a systematic review of the l — a 2008 science paper on RAS in lung cancer. It reviews the RAS research. The paper is the RAS review: the findings on lung ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2453330: The insulator binding protein CTCF positions 20 nucleosomes around its binding sites across the — a 2008 science paper on CTCF's bead game. It maps the bead placement for labs. The paper is the bead study: the notes on CTCF, filed here in full session today.
