prichard-masonry-dissected-1730:
Samuel Prichard, a disaffected former Mason, published Masonry Dissected in London in 1730. The pamphlet sets out the catechism of the three Craft degrees in plain question and answer. It is the first and most famous Masonic exposé, and it founded the literature of exposure that has followed the fraternity ever since.

Prichard claims to print what lodges swore their members to hide. His catechism runs through signs, words, and the story of Hiram in order. Masons denounced him, and the public bought the pamphlet eagerly. Historians still treat it as the era's best evidence for early ritual. Few exposures have been reprinted so often or believed so widely.
perjurd-free-mason-detected-1730:
The Perjur'd Free Mason Detected appeared in London in 1730, the same year as Prichard's Masonry Dissected. It answers Prichard directly. The author signs himself a Free Mason and writes in righteous anger at the betrayal of the fraternity's secrets, calling the exposer perjured for breaking his obligation.

The pamphlet is the earliest Masonic counter-pamphlet in print. It defends the Craft's honor and disputes the exposé's claims point by point. As the fraternity's first printed self-defense, it holds a pivotal place. The quarrel shows Masonry learning to fight in the new arena of cheap print. Both pamphlets together stage the birth of a very modern argument about secrecy.
plos-pone-0004930:
People feel what others feel more strongly when those others seem similar. Andrea Serino, Giulia Giovagnoli and Elisabetta Làdavas examined this effect in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tested whether social representation shapes shared feeling. Social representation is how the brain pictures another person.

Judged similarity can rest on physical traits. It can also rest on group membership, such as ethnic or political identity. The study tested whether similarity changes how strongly states are shared. Its results speak to the biology of empathy. They also bear on why group divisions can dull our response to other people's pain.
plos-pone-0005030:
Cells crawl by spending energy at their leading edge. That energy is ATP, the cell's fuel. Jan Kuiper and colleagues studied a local fuel source in PLOS ONE in 2009. The source is brain-type creatine kinase, or CK-B. The enzyme transfers high-energy phosphate groups between ATP and phosphocreatine.

CK-B makes ATP right where the cell moves. Local generation facilitates cell motility. Fuel made far away would arrive too slowly. Deficiency of CK-B is coupled to lost function in neural circuits. The finding explains how moving cells keep energy close. It connects an old energy enzyme to the mechanics of crawling.
plos-pone-0005130:
Fascin-1 bundles actin into spikes that help cells move. It is absent from most normal epithelia. Many carcinomas switch it on, and its presence predicts poor outcomes. Yosuke Hashimoto and colleagues asked what turns its gene on. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied the fascin-1 promoter in human carcinoma cells.

Two regulators control that promoter. One is CREB, a common gene switch. The other is the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, a sensor for environmental chemicals. Together they drive fascin-1 expression in these cancer cells. The switches reveal how cancers arm their invasion tool. Blocking them could blunt spread. The finding also links chemical sensing to cancer cell movement.
plos-pone-0005230:
Nerve cells send messages by releasing packets from tiny vesicles, and a protein family called SV2 rides on those vesicles. One member, SV2B, is the most distinct of the three forms in mammals. Morgans and colleagues studied mice lacking SV2B in PLOS ONE in 2009, focusing on the retina.

Without SV2B, signaling in the retina grew weaker, as the title states. The mix of other vesicle proteins also changed. The results show this quiet vesicle protein matters for crisp signaling in the eye, and they guide work on how release sites are stocked.
plos-pone-0005330:
People who eat deer killed with lead bullets may swallow lead fragments along with the meat. Studies of subsistence hunters have shown raised blood lead levels, and ammunition residues persist in carcasses. Hunt and colleagues examined venison from rifle-killed deer in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study assessed how much lead bullet fragments contribute to human dietary exposure. Even small fragments matter, since lead harms nerves and development at low doses. The findings inform hunters, processors, and health advisers about a risk that is invisible in the meat. Lead does its worst harm to the young brain, so meat shared with kids. With women who may bear kids is where this quiet risk should be cut first and with most care.
plos-pone-0005930:
A tuberculosis vaccine can fail or succeed on dose alone. Claus Aagaard, Truc Hoang, Angelo Izzo and colleagues showed that in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of the vaccine Ag85B-TB10.4 given with the adjuvant IC31. Earlier work had paired the same vaccine with a different adjuvant built on charged fat particles.

With IC31, protection against the bacteria and the rise of hard-working T cells both hinged heavily on how much antigen was given. Dose is thus a dial that can tune the whole vaccine. The finding tells trial designers that picking the amount is as vital as picking the ingredients, a lesson for TB vaccines still in testing.
plos-pone-0006030:
Psoriasis patches almost never turn into skin cancer, a fact that puzzles doctors. Sari Suomela, Outi Elomaa, Tiina Skoog and colleagues followed one gene from that puzzle in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies CCHCR1, a gene inside the main psoriasis risk region, which is switched on in some cancers, and looks at its levels in skin cancer.

CCHCR1 is up-regulated in skin cancer and tied to expression of EGFR, a growth receptor, the title reports. A psoriasis gene with a second life in cancer links two skin stories that seemed opposed. The work may help explain the strange guard psoriasis offers, and it adds a fresh suspect to the study of skin tumors.
plos-pone-0006130:
A coronavirus enters cells by its spike, and small changes there can rewrite its reach. Yoshiyuki Yamada, Xiao Bo Liu, Shou Guo Fang and colleagues proved that in cultured cells in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the avian coronavirus infectious bronchitis virus, adapted to eggs and to chicken and monkey kidney cells, and the spike protein substitutions it gained along the way.

Gaining cell-cell fusion activity through those substitutions determined whether the virus could infect, the title reports. Entry is the first gate every virus must pass, so its rules are basic to outbreak science. The work shows how a poultry virus tunes its key, a lesson that reads across the whole coronavirus family.
plos-pone-0006230:
Music feels stronger with eyes closed, and Yulia Lerner and colleagues wanted to know why. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study links the effect to the amygdala, a brain region tied to emotion. The value people feel from a stimulus depends partly on how the brain is processing at that moment.

Brain imaging showed the amygdala mediating the boost in emotional experience when eyes stay shut. Context, not just sound, sets the strength of feeling. The finding helps explain everyday habits like closing eyes at concerts. It also guides studies of emotion, which must account for such processing styles.
plos-pone-0006730:
Tao Dao and colleagues hunted for immune targets on a common cancer protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is cyclin D1, overproduced in many human tumors. Excess cyclin D1 helps drive uncontrolled cell division. That makes it a possible target antigen for immunotherapy. Only a few T cell targets on it were known.

The team identified a human cyclin D1 peptide that triggers killer-helping T cells. The peptide induced human cytotoxic CD4 T cells. CD4 cells are usually helpers, so cytotoxic ones are notable weapons. A defined peptide target could support vaccine-style cancer treatments. The work widens the list of cyclin D1 fragments the immune system can be taught to attack.
plos-pone-0006830:
Fang Chen and Yongqun He studied how a rough strain of Brucella kills mouse macrophages in PLOS ONE in 2009. Brucella bacteria live inside host cells and cause brucellosis. Surviving inside macrophages is critical for chronic infection. Smooth virulent strains block the death of their host cells. Rough strains behave differently.

The rough Brucella abortus strain induced both apoptotic and necrotic death. An enzyme called caspase-2 mediated the killing. The contrast with smooth strains highlights a survival strategy. Blocking cell death lets smooth bacteria persist quietly. Understanding the switch may expose ways to break chronic brucellosis.
plos-pone-0006930:
Stefanie Müller, Monika Götz, and Dagmar Beier studied acid sensing in a stomach bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium was Helicobacter pylori, a human gastric pathogen. Its ArsRS two-component system is the master regulator of acid adaptation. Low pH was thought to trigger the sensor protein ArsS into action.

The team focused on one building block of ArsS, histidine residue ninety-four. They tested whether that single residue does the pH sensing. Pinpointing the sensor helps explain how the bacterium survives stomach acid. That survival is the first step in infections that can lead to ulcers and stomach cancer.
plos-pone-0007030:
Shelton Bradrick and Matthias Gromeier identified a new cap-binding protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. RNA made by RNA polymerase II carries a special cap at its start. The cap is a modified building block called 7-methylguanosine. Proteins that grip this cap help control the RNA's fate, from export to translation.

The authors showed that a protein named Gemin5 binds this cap. That was a new role for a protein known from other RNA work. Cap binding places Gemin5 at a control point for gene expression. The finding may reshape views of how messenger RNA is handled.
plos-pone-0007130:
Sean Rice and Anthony Papadopoulos modelled chance in evolution in PLOS ONE in 2009. The movement of animals and plants between local groups shapes how species adapt and split. It also helps keep gene variety alive. That movement is not a steady flow, and part of it is pure chance. Fitness, too, can shift by luck from year to year.

Their model joined chance in fitness with chance in movement. It asked how the double dose of luck changes the fate of groups. Fixed models can mislead when groups are small and luck looms large. This work gives a more honest base for how species change over time.
plos-pone-0007230:
Lluís Armengol, Sergi Villatoro, Juan R. González, and colleagues searched human genomes for group-defining differences in 2009. Understanding genetic contributions to trait variation matters for health. Populations differ in disease risk and in response to medicines, and genetics explains part of those differences.

The authors profile structural variation across the genome. They focus on copy number variants, stretches of DNA gained or lost between people. They identify variants that define genomic differences among major human groups. Their catalog helps researchers study population history and plan medical genetics studies more fairly.
plos-pone-0007330:
Hong-Wen Liu, Yun-Cin Luo, Chia-Lin Ho, and colleagues studied how cells follow their substrate in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cells navigate by soluble chemical gradients, but that guidance fades if the signal stays unchanged. Whether guidance by the extracellular matrix, the material cells crawl on, also adapts was obscure.

The authors test locomotion guidance by immobilized matrix cues. They report the guidance is adaptive, like chemical guidance. They also show a transient change in calcium levels can restore faded guidance. Their finding reveals a reset mechanism for cells moving through tissues.

plos-pone-0006330:
Potassium channels that open near a neuron's resting voltage help set how excitable the cell is. plos-pone-0009730:
Fibrocytes are blood-born cells that help build scar tissue after injury. S. John Curnow and colleagues grew them from mononuclear blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. They compared growth with serum present and with serum absent. Mononuclear cells include the white blood cells that patrol the body.

This paper refines those predictions: it starts from the liquid-drop model of the nucleus and applies physics-guided corrections to the leftover error. The authors show the corrected half-life estimates match measured data more closely.

arxiv-2601-08530: Zhonghao Wang, Junqiang Peng, Yuxi Liu, and Mingyu Xiao ask how hard it is to rig a knockout tournament. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines the tournament fixing problem on a tournament digraph. The digraph encodes outcomes of all possible matches, and a designated favorite must emerge as champion. The question is whether a schedule exists that guarantees that result. The authors study the case where few players can beat or be beaten by the favorite. Complexity results here inform fair bracket design in sports and esports.
arxiv-2601-06630:
Molla Basir Ahamed, Sujoy Majumder, and Nabadwip Sarkar sharpen Bohr-type inequalities in 2026. They study multidimensional analogues for bounded holomorphic mappings in several variables. Their domain is the unit polydisc in complex space.

They establish a sharp extension of the classical Bohr inequality. The Bohr radius remains one over three n, they prove. That radius holds for functions bounded by unity in the multivariate setting. Classical Bohr results concern power series in one complex variable. Extending them sharply to many variables is delicate and long studied. Their radius matches the best possible value, hence sharp. Complex analysts get a definitive constant for the polydisc case. Euler operators enter their treatment of Schwarz functions as well.
arxiv-2601-07530:
Yi Liao, Quan-Yu Wang, and Yuanbin Wu study a scattering process where particles carry a twist. Their 2026 preprint concerns electron-positron annihilation into two photons. In this setup the positron is a plane wave, while the electron and photons are vortex states. Vortex states carry orbital angular momentum, like a corkscrew. The geometry is off-axis, adding further structure.

The authors build a theoretical formalism for this triple-vortex process. With it they examine how vortex parameters and the scattering angle affect the outcome. Vortex beams of particles and light are a growing tool in fundamental physics. Understanding their collisions may open new ways to probe particle properties. The paper is written for specialists in quantum electrodynamics and structured beams.
arxiv-2601-07730:
Jithin D. George and colleagues integrate equations along paths in the complex plane instead of the real line. Most numerical time-stepping methods use real-valued steps. Complex steps add a degree of freedom, since size can be chosen in both real and imaginary directions. Their 2026 preprint shows that specific complex paths expand the stability region. Larger stability regions mean bigger, safer steps for stiff problems.

The advantage is clearest for complex-valued systems. Stiff problems force tiny steps in standard methods because fast and slow scales coexist. A clever path can sidestep some of that cost. The authors present explicit integrators built on this idea. Numerical analysts solving stiff differential equations are the readers. The work turns an old curiosity, complex time, into practical integrators.
arxiv-2601-07830:
Valentina Njaradi, Rodrigo Carrasco-Davis, and Peter Latham ask how a learner should schedule its own learning rate. Learning efficiently is a basic challenge for both biological and artificial agents. Speed brings rapid improvement but also costs: effort, instability, and resource use. Their 2026 preprint studies the optimal schedule that balances effort against performance. The learning rate here is the size of each update step.

Too fast, and learning can thrash or waste energy. Too slow, and time runs out before mastery. A principled schedule could guide both animal learning studies and machine learning practice. The authors come from computational neuroscience, where brains are the original self-tuning learners. Their framing treats the schedule as a decision problem. The paper speaks to neuroscientists and machine learning scholars who tune learning dynamics.
arxiv-2601-07930:
Liying Zhang and Liang Zhao use a transformer model to swap groups in molecules on its own. Swapping a functional group is a key approach in cheminformatics to design compounds with set traits. Old methods for removal and swaps rely on rules of thumb set by hand. Those rules limit the diversity and novelty of the structures produced. Their 2026 preprint gives a transformer approach to the task.

Such models learn from data in place of hand set rules. Applied to molecules, they propose swaps a rule book would never suggest. Drug chemists use such swaps to tune strength, safety, and how a drug dissolves. Novel structures matter because patented and known chemical space is crowded. The paper serves scholars of cheminformatics and drug search teams. It brings a language model architecture to a classic molecular design step. A good swap keeps what works and trims what harms.
arxiv-2601-07130:
Nicholas Pritchard, Richard Dodson, and Andreas Wicenec wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a new kind of chip for radio astronomy. The chips are called neuromorphic, which means they work in a way shaped by the brain. Radio work leans on custom, trial-based tools built for each task. The next wave of telescopes will push those tools hard.

Two vast arrays lead that wave. One is the Square Kilometre Array, or SKA. The other is the next-generation Very Large Array, or ngVLA. Both will draw huge amounts of power. Both face harsh radio noise from human tech. With classic von Neumann designs, the power bill may block the science goals. Brain-shaped chips use far less power per task. The authors weigh what that shift could mean for the labs that run these telescopes. They ask where such chips could help first and most.
arxiv-2601-07230:
A 2026 arXiv paper in pure math sets out a new form of cohomology for groups. Cohomology reads the shape of a space or a group by means of chains and holes. The new form is called configured group cohomology. It grows out of a known form called locally smooth cohomology. Its parts are tuples in a good layout, with shapes that fill the gaps.

The frame yields new 3-cocycles of Chern-Simons type, which take values in the real line split by whole steps, written as R over Z. They live on groups of diffeomorphisms, smooth maps that bend a shape but do not tear it. The maps in view keep a set geometric form in place. The paper also deals with torsion in the third homology of such groups, with values in Q over Z.
arxiv-2601-08630: Gregoire Nadin, David Nahmani, and Nicolas Vauchelet wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the best way to swap one population for a new one. The work treats an optimal control problem. The system is ruled by a nonlinear differential equation with a bistable term that repeats in time. Bistable means the system can rest in one of two states. The model tracks A-type members as B-type members take their place, in a setting that shifts over time. The state is the share of B-type members in the group.
arxiv-2601-08930:
Enhyeok Jang and five co-authors study a quantum chip shaped like a race track. On such a chip, trapped ions move round zones where work is done. A past test on this shape showed a quantum edge for pure chance tasks. The team asks how well the shape runs plain programs as zones are added.

They run test programs that tune a set of values by trial. To their own surprise, more zones can make runs slow, not fast. The blame lies in the plan that sets which job goes to which zone, and when. A reader who builds such chips gets a clear warn. More zones help only if the work plan grows with them.
arxiv-2601-09030:
Yingtong Zhu and five co-authors explain a strange glow from a thin sheet of a sulfur based stuff. The sheet is one layer of WS2. Its glow comes from a bound pair of a charge and a gap, called an exciton. The pair spans two low zones of the sheet. When the sheet is stretched both ways, the glow shifts in a wave like path.

Past lab work saw that wave path, but not its cause. The team builds a joint frame that plays the glow back in full. It shows how stretch mixes the two zones to steer the pair. A reader in thin stuffs gets a cause for a known glow quirk, and a knob to tune it.
arxiv-2601-09330:
Pierrot Lamontagne and a large team weigh a small planet round a near red dwarf star, GJ 3090. The planet, GJ 3090 b, is a sub-Neptune: large than Earth, small than Neptune. It crosses its star each 2.85 days. New speed marks from the NIRPS tool, plus past HARPS marks, let the team pin its mass with more care.

They set the mass at a value near four and a half Earth masses, with a tight doubt range. They also find a next planet near the star's own spin span. That find needs care, since star spin can fake a planet mark. A reader in planet work gets a firm mass for a key near case, and a warn on its mate.
arxiv-2601-10230:
Ming Liu and Yosuke Hasegawa sim flows past a spinning solid with odd shape. Such flows drive fans, pumps, and turbines. A true sim is hard when the solid spins and its shape is bent. The team use a volume penalty method to fake the solid.

They pair the method with two frame tricks. One frame spins with the solid. One mesh slides past the next. Each pair gives a way to host a spinning shape on a fixed grid. The paper tests both pairs. It aims for sims that are sharp yet cheap to run.
arxiv-2601-10430:
L. Serafini and a large team plan to probe fault zones with muon beams. Muons are heavy kin of electrons. A high energy beam of them can pass through rock. The team want to send such a beam across a live fault. Rock at a fault can act as a piezo stuff under stress.

Such stuff gives off charge when squeezed. A muon beam could read that charge at depth. The paper grows a past study of the plan. It sets out the beam and the read gear it would need. The aim is a new probe of stress in fault zones.
arxiv-2601-10630:
A 2026 arXiv preprint takes up classification imbalance, the case where one class is far rarer than the other. Rare classes arise in fraud, disease, and fault detection. A model trained on skewed data may do well on the common class and fail on the rare one. The authors reframe the problem to handle that skew head on.

They cast it as transfer learning under label shift. The source data follow the skewed mix seen in practice. The target is a balanced mix, the one used to judge performance. That frame clarifies what a fair test should look like. It gives practitioners a principled way to train and score models when classes are far from even.
arxiv-2601-10830:
Ayman Badawi defines a new graph from a finite abelian group. Take a group H with at least two elements, and an integer m above one. Make each group element a vertex. Join two vertices when the m-th power of one equals the other element in the right pairing. The result is the m-graph of H.

Graphs built from groups let algebra be seen and counted. Degrees, cliques, and connected parts can mirror subgroup structure. Badawi's construction adds a fresh member to this family. Papers of this kind supply test cases for graph theory and new lenses for finite group structure at the same time.
arxiv-2601-10930:
Zhixian Xie, Yu Xiang, Michael Posa, and Wanxin Jin build a framework for dexterous robot manipulation over long horizons. Contact-rich tasks demand joint reasoning about shape, joint limits, and rough contact dynamics. End-to-end learned policies skip that structure. They often need huge data, transfer poorly from simulation, and generalize weakly across tasks and robot bodies.

The authors combine reinforcement learning with model predictive control in a hierarchy. Their frame is geometry-aware: where to touch, and how to make contact, are decided as linked questions. The hierarchy lets learning handle what models miss, and models keep learning grounded. The work targets hands that must work in the real world, not just in simulators.
arxiv-2601-11130:
Tatiana M. Rodríguez and co-authors present very-long-baseline views of ionized jets from young stars. The team used the VLA at 1.3 centimeters with sub-arcsecond resolution, about a tenth of an arcsecond. They also observed the 22.2 gigahertz water maser line. Targets were fifteen compact radio sources with rising spectral index, plus eight string-like radio structures from earlier surveys.

Rising spectra and string shapes are signs of jets carving through natal gas. Sub-arcsecond maps can separate a true jet from a round wind. Maser spots mark shocked gas along the flow. Such detail shows how jets launch and collimate, a core step in star birth that also feeds back on the cloud that made the star.
arxiv-2601-11830:
Griselda Arroyo-Chávez, Enrique Vázquez-Semadeni, and James Wurster ask what sets spin in giant gas clouds in space. Such clouds form stars, and their spin shapes how stars and disks form. Views show that spin per unit mass grows with size in a set pattern.

They weigh three forces: gravity, turbulence, and magnetic fields. Each can move spin from large scales to small ones, or the other way. Their work tests which force rules the pattern seen in the views. The answer helps star birth models start from more true cloud states.
arxiv-2601-12030:
Yilun Yao, Shan Huang, Elsie Dai, and their co-authors keep long AI research tasks on track. Language models used as research agents lose skill as their chat history grows. That decay, called context rot, breaks clear, task-fit inner state over long runs.

Their frame, called ARC in the work, manages context with active picks and self-review. It aims to keep key facts and drop noise as a task runs. Long search and report tasks stand to gain most. The work tests how such care lifts long-run agent skill.  Less rot means more sound work on long search tasks.
arxiv-2601-12230:
Koki Takahashi and Shun Watanabe prove channel resolvability for classical-quantum channels by a set code method. Resolvability asks how well random noise can mimic a channel output. Past proofs for such channels used random coding alone.

Their past work gave a deterministic proof for classic channels via multiplicative weights. They extend that route with a matrix form of the weights method. A set code is easier to build and audit than a random one. The result adds a firm tool to quantum information theory.  A set proof is a step past random code proofs.
arxiv-2601-11330:
A hunt for dark matter with a Higgs boson is reported in this preprint. The authors are listed as the CMS team in the record. The data come from proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The collision energy is 13 TeV, the standard LHC run energy.

The sought event pairs dark matter with one Higgs boson. The Higgs then decays to a bottom quark pair. That decay is common, which gives the hunt more events. Data from the CMS detector total 101 inverse femtobarns. Dark matter would flee the detector unseen, as missing energy. A Higgs tag plus missing energy is thus the signature. The search tests models where the Higgs links to a dark sector.
arxiv-2601-11630:
Haonan Wei and five coauthors distill a generation model to one layer. Their 2026 preprint reworks FreeFlow, a one-step flow method. Flow matching compresses diffusion generation into few steps. MeanFlow and FreeFlow lead that one-step push via ODEs.

FreeFlow uses a 28-layer transformer for its generation. The team reads those layers as steps of an Euler scheme. Depth acts as discrete time along an ODE path. That view suggests the layers can be re-distilled. Their model generates in one step with a single-layer transformer. A one-layer generator cuts cost and latency sharply. The work tests how much depth generation truly needs.
arxiv-2601-13330:
Jamie Cummins, Beth Clarke, Ian Hussey, and Malte Elson built a tool to check if a paper matches its pre plan. A pre plan, called a registration, states what a study will do before it starts. Across social and health fields, pre plans aid clear and strict science. Yet checks of plans are rare, so their worth is lost.

Their tool is called RegCheck. It pairs a study plan with its paper and flags where they part. Parts may be swaps in tests, marks, or who took part. By auto of the pair work, checks can run at scale. For journals and funders, the tool turns a norm few check into one that can be kept.
arxiv-2601-13530:
Tomoya Hayata, Yoshimasa Hidaka, and Yuta Kikuchi watch a deformed Yang-Mills theory start to thermalize on a trapped ion quantum computer. Non balance acts of quantum many body systems are a top aim of quantum sims. Gauge theories in high energy physics draw more and more such runs as gear grows.

Yet most past runs stay in one space dim, or in Abelian theories like the Schwinger model and the toric code. The team runs a q deformed SU(2) theory, a non Abelian case with a twist. They track when thermal acts set in. Such a run tests if today's ion gear can host the gauge acts that count most.
arxiv-2601-12430:
Tsan Tsai Chan and four co authors study a quirk of vision language models. These models take in a system prompt, an image, and text, then answer questions. A known flaw is hallucination, where the model claims things that are not there. Such flaws are often linked to how attention is split across the three inputs.

Most fixes so far push the model to attend more to the image. The team argue that this image centric view misses the roles of the other inputs. Their title names the effect they find: system mediated attention gaps make models say yes. In other words, the system prompt can tilt a model toward agreement. That tilt helps explain false yes answers on visual questions.
arxiv-2601-12730:
Zhaochun Li and six co authors rethink the exploration and exploitation trade off in reinforcement learning for language models. Training with group relative policy optimization tends to be exploitation driven. Entropy falls steadily, samples converge, and exploration fades away. A model that stops exploring can lock into mediocre habits.

Most existing fixes are sample centric, hunting or rewarding rare samples. They assume exploration comes from novel trajectories and tokens. The team argue for a distribution centric policy optimization instead. Their title claims this view dominates the old trade off framing. Shifting focus from single samples to whole distributions may keep exploration alive. The work targets a core weakness in current language model training.
arxiv-2601-12930:
Jale Basten, Katja Ickstadt, and Nina Timmesfeld guide analysis of stepped wedge cluster trials. In these trials, all clusters start in the control condition. They cross over to the intervention on a staggered schedule over time. Sequential measurements within clusters span multiple periods.

That staggered start unbalances observations across intervention groups over time. Individual time effects can then bias naive analyses of the treatment effect. The team run a simulation study on how to address those effects. Guidance grounded in simulation helps trialists pick sound models in advance. Stepped wedge designs are common in health service research. Their advice serves a wide base of applied statisticians.
arxiv-2601-13730:
Makoto Ueki studies how epidemics break out in populations split into linked groups in 2026. During an outbreak, a pathogen spreads through host groups that interact. Group size, network shape, and the strength of links all shape the spread. Ueki uses stochastic simulation, which rolls random events, and analytic approximations.

The work shows how outbreak sizes depend on those three factors. Network architecture can speed or slow a wave of cases. Coupling strength sets how fast one group seeds the next. Such maps help planners guard the links that matter most.
arxiv-2601-14030:
Samuel Remedios and co-authors sharpen MRI scans by combining many images at once in 2026. Diffusion models are the current state of the art for imaging inverse problems. They sample from a prior distribution to fill in missing detail. A known likelihood function then guides posterior sampling without retraining.

Most methods focus on single-image inverse problems. Multi-image MRI super-resolution must fuse several scans of one subject. Their likelihood-separable diffusion inference targets that multi-image case. Sharper MRI from faster, lower-grade scans could cut patient time in the scanner. Most past work used one scan at a time. Real clinics have many scans per case, so the multi-image case is the one that counts.
arxiv-2601-14130:
Till Aczel and co-authors compress gray images with logic circuits that learn in 2026. Neural image codecs beat traditional hand-crafted methods like PNG in compression ratio. They often incur substantial computational overhead to do so. That overhead limits deployment on energy-constrained devices like smartphones, cameras, and drones.

Their GIC-DLC trains lookup tables to mix neural flexibility with Boolean efficiency. Differentiable logic circuits learn the compression while staying hardware-friendly. The codec targets grayscale images in this work. Small devices could then store more photos on less power. Logic steps use far less power than dense math units. On a drone or a phone, that saved power is pure gain.
arxiv-2601-14230:
Yiyang Wang, Yiqiao Jin, Alex Cabral, and Josiah Hester build companion agents that keep distinct voices in 2026. Multi-agent systems have emerged as socio-collaborative companions for emotional and cognitive support. Such systems frequently suffer from persona collapse. Agents revert to generic, homogenized assistant behaviors over time.

Social sycophancy is an other flaw, producing redundant, non-constructive dialogue. Their Mascot framework targets multi-agent socio-collaborative companion systems. It is designed to be generalizable across uses. Companions that stay in character could give richer, more honest support. The frame aims to keep each agent's voice its own. It also aims to curb praise that adds heat but no light to the talk.
arxiv-2601-14730:
Bizu Feng, Zhimu Yang, Shaode Yu, and Zixin Hu explain graph neural network predictions in this 2026 paper. Despite the widespread success of graph neural networks, understanding the reasons behind their specific predictions remains challenging. Existing explainability methods face a trade-off. Gradient-based approaches are computationally efficient but often ignore structural interactions.

Game-theoretic techniques capture interactions, but at high computational overhead. They may also deviate from the model's true reasoning path. Their explainer, FSX, is enhanced by message flow sensitivity. It tracks how messages move through the graph to shape a prediction. The path it picks can be shown. A user can ask why, and get an answer tied to the graph. Readers get explanations that follow the network's own traffic, at a cost closer to the fast methods.
arxiv-2601-15630:
Chandra Prakash, Mary Lind, and Avneesh Sisodia write on governing AI agents in health care in a 2026 arXiv paper. Health systems now embed agentic AI in daily workflows. Uses include clinical documentation support and early-warning monitoring. As agents spread across departments and vendors, sprawl sets in. Duplicated agents appear. Accountability blurs. Controls vary from team to team. Tool permissions can outlive the task they were granted for.

The authors address the full lifecycle of such agents, per the title. Governance means knowing which agents exist, who owns them, and what they may touch. Lifecycle management covers launch, updates, and retirement. For hospitals, the stakes are clinical, not just technical. A stray agent with stale permissions is a safety risk. The paper speaks to leaders who must tame agent growth.
arxiv-2601-15730:
E. García-Río, R. Rodríguez-Gigirey, and R. Vázquez-Lorenzo describe a class of geometric structures in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is four-dimensional Lorentzian algebraic Ricci solitons. A Ricci soliton is a space whose metric evolves in a self-similar way. Lorentzian geometry adds a time direction, as in relativity. The authors contrast their setting with the Riemannian one. There, such solitons are far more restricted.

In their setting, a striking fact holds. Any connected, simply connected four-dimensional Lie group admits a left-invariant Lorentz metric that is a Ricci soliton. That breadth is unexpected next to the Riemannian case. Classification work like this maps what geometries can exist. Relativity and geometry both draw on such maps when they model spacetime.
arxiv-2601-14830:
Monalisa Dubey, Kuntal Misra, and a large team of co-authors report on a star that blew up in the galaxy NGC 2139. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the supernova SN 2023zcu, classed as a Type IIP event. The team tracked it with both light data and spectra.

The light curve is well sampled from the rise through the flat plateau phase and into the late nebular phase. The authors measure an optically thick phase of about 100 days. The title also points to early flash features seen near the start of the event.
arxiv-2601-15030:
Piotr Płonka and Agnieszka Janiuk model the death of a massive spinning star. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions known. Long bursts come from stars that collapse into black holes.

At collapse, the new black hole holds far less mass than the star left behind. The rest of the star still falls in or flies out as a jet. The team runs three-dimensional simulations in general relativity with magnetic fields. Their runs follow how the jet forms deep inside and pushes out through the star.
arxiv-2601-15230:
Edgar F. A. Lederer checks two classic Turing machines with a modern proof tool. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with formal verification in Dafny, a program verifier. Both machines are deciders, so the goal is total correctness, not just partial results.

The machines are typical first examples from courses in theoretical computer science. The second one is taken straight from a standard textbook on the subject. Lederer proves each machine halts with the right answer on every input. The paper shows how Dafny handles these textbook cases from start to finish.
arxiv-2601-16130:
Neeley Pate and coauthors test if language models copy slanted thought in humans. Their 2026 preprint deals with driven thought, where a wish bends how facts are read. Human tests show this bend in clear ways. It is not known if plain language models show the same bend. The team reruns human tests with models in the place of people.

They check if model picks shift with the wish as human picks do. Like shifts would mean models pick up human bias from text. Un like shifts would mark a gap in how models think. The work helps teams judge model acts in charged topics. It ties model tests to known human test designs.
arxiv-2601-16230:
Aditya Kamlesh and coauthors test speech models on scores for learned tongue speech. Their 2026 preprint deals with scores for speech in a second tongue. Good scores give fair feed back and track growth. Speech must be judged on flow, tune and full sense at once. That joint score task is hard for code tools.

The team tests speech large models with no task train. Such zero shot tests show what the models can do at once. They weigh scores across all parts of speech grade. Gaps show where fresh train or cues are needed. The work maps a path to fair speech scores.
arxiv-2601-16430:
David King, Thomas Russell and Ahmad Omar show how live grains shake a soft sheet. Their 2026 preprint deals with a sheet that bends with ease. Live grains swim or crawl and push on the sheet. The team solves for the push those grains place on it. That push turns out to cut the pull tight of the sheet.

It also cuts the bend stiff of the sheet as a whole. New far reach terms join spots on the sheet through the grains. Such terms have no match in dead sheet maths. Soft sheets in cells may act by these same rules. The work gives a first theory for the pair.
arxiv-2601-16730:
Bekir Daniş and İsmail Alperen Öğüt settle a math guess with a firm no. The guess claimed that all posets have a trait called conclusiveness. A poset is a set with a part-way rank rule. Their 2026 preprint gives a case that breaks the guess. The case leans on twist traits and a famed flat shape.

The authors also sort which small posets hold the trait. They link the trait to the life of outer derivations. Such maps track how a rank rule can shift. Plain cases that break broad guesses are gold in math. They keep the field from years of false trails.
arxiv-2601-16830:
Andrew Thompson and Miles McCrory work out exact math for doubt in neural nets. A trained net gives a call for each input. When inputs blur, the call's blur counts too. Past work gauged that blur with rough series tricks. Their 2026 preprint gives exact forms for one class of nets.

The nets have one hidden layer and a ramp-style switch. Inputs are set as bell-shaped chance spreads. From those, exact mean and spread of the output fall out. No rough cuts are used in the proof. Exact doubt helps in care, flight, and risk work. It lets teams trust net calls with proof, not hope.
arxiv-2601-17030:
Maxwell Siegel broadens his own past frame for Collatz-type tasks. The Collatz task asks if a simple rule chain always lands at one. Hydra maps are kin rules that branch like the myth beast. His 2026 preprint casts those maps on rings of whole marks. Those rings sit in global fields, a broad number world.

His frame joins the maps to ghost-value spread math. That math, from his 2024 work, reads how marks spread. Broad frames may crack more than one hard task. They show how one rule set can span many fields. Pure number work gains a wider lens here.
arxiv-2601-17130:
Megha Khosla asks how graph shape sways leak risk in graph neural nets. Such nets learn from webs of linked facts. They ace tasks like node tags and link calls. But they may leak if a fact was in their train set. Foes can probe that leak with sly asks. Her 2026 preprint ties the leak risk to the web's shape.

Dense hubs and tight crowds may leak more than loose webs. Shape-wise maps can warn where leaks run high. Health and bank webs need such warns most. Their facts are the most dear if leaked. This work gives builders a shape check for risk.
arxiv-2601-17330:
Laurent Caraffa asks if common training tricks share one deep rule. Machine learning uses weight decay, dropout, and moving averages to keep models in check. Each trick works, yet each rests on its own story. At the same time, training big models burns more and more energy. Caraffa asks if learning nears a hard efficiency bound.

He frames best regularization under information-geometric constraints. That frame ties the tricks to limits from thermodynamics. If such a bound holds, it would guide greener training. It would also unite split tricks in one theory. The work is a step toward learning rules set by physics, not just trial and error.
arxiv-2601-17430:
Zichuan Yang and Yiming Xing study how to find a bad subset among many data streams. The streams have correlated noise, so one odd stream can drag its kin. Uses include monitoring and security in cyber-physical systems. The task is a form of combinatorial pure exploration. Each stream acts like an arm to test. Measures must be spent in sequence under doubt.

Smart spending finds the anomaly with fewer checks. Correlation can help or mislead that hunt. The authors frame active tests that learn as they go. Faster finds mean faster response to faults or attacks. The work fits plants, grids, and sensor nets. It treats search cost as part of the problem.
arxiv-2601-17530:
Gautam Siddharth Kashyap and co-authors present ConLLM for spotting multi-modal deepfakes. Deepfake tools now fake video, audio, and text at once. Fakes threaten trust in news, courts, and daily talk. Single-mode detectors miss cross-mode clues. The authors aim at fakes that span modes. Their system uses a language model at its core, as the name ConLLM states.

Cross-mode checks can catch what one stream hides. A voice may not match lip work or text tone. Tools that fuse those signs raise the bar for fakes. The work serves platforms and newsrooms that vet media fast. It adds to a growing shield against synthetic fraud.
arxiv-2601-17730:
Ting-Yan Li, Zi-Yue Bai, and Xiang Liu study a hard corner of particle physics in this 2026 preprint. They look at how high-spin mesons form when a pion hits a proton. The mesons in question are the omega and rho families with spin values of three, four, and five. States with such high spin are rare and hard to pin down.

The team uses an effective Lagrangian method to work out how these mesons are made. That method turns the forces between particles into terms that can be solved step by step. The study covers each spin value in turn, so the states can be compared side by side. Work like this gives experimenters a clearer guide for searches at hadron facilities.
arxiv-2601-17830:
Mengmeng Wang and co-authors work on making diffusion models cheaper to train. Their 2026 preprint presents VAE-REPA, a method for diffusion transformers. These models build images by clearing noise step by step, and they perform well. Their training, though, converges slowly. Past fixes lean on outside encoders or on running two models at once, and both add heavy cost.

VAE-REPA instead aligns the model's inner features with those of a variational autoencoder. That gives the training a guide that is already inside a light setup. The aim is faster convergence without the extra weight of external parts. Cheaper training matters as these models grow in size and use.
arxiv-2601-17930:
Antonio Falcó, Daniela Falcó-Pomares, and Hermann G. Matthies give a strict, self-contained proof of a key quantum method. Their 2026 preprint covers the Grover-Rudolph state preparation algorithm. Many quantum methods need a state whose heights encode a known probability list. Loading such a state is a basic first step for tasks like amplitude estimation. The Grover-Rudolph method builds that state step by step from the list.

A proof that stands alone, with each step checked, serves students and builders alike. It also guards against hidden gaps in a much-used method. The authors lay out the full argument in one place. Readers can verify the method without chasing other sources. That kind of care keeps core tools sound.
arxiv-2601-18030:
Markus N. Rabe, Judith Clymo, and Zheren Dong give language models a sense of spelling. Their 2026 preprint changes the embedding layer, the part that turns tokens into numbers. The change feeds each token's letters into its embedding. Models trained this way do better not only on spelling tasks but across standard tests as well. The team runs scaling studies with models from forty million to eight hundred million parameters.

Spelling is usually invisible to a model that sees only whole tokens. That blindness hurts on names, rare words, and typos. Letter-aware embeddings attack the problem at the root. The gains across broad tests suggest the fix helps general skill, not just spelling bees.
arxiv-2601-18930:
Seiji Shaw and three co-authors teach agents to learn worlds they cannot fully see. In such worlds, called POMDPs, the true state stays hidden and the agent sees only partial clues. Their test cases include things like locking mechanisms, where the inner state is not shown.

The agent starts out knowing what acts it can take and what it might observe. It does not know the states, how they change, or how clues link to states. Learning past those limits would let robots and software cope with hidden machinery in the real world, not just in clean lab setups.
arxiv-2601-19130:
Zexu Pan and four co-authors pull one voice from a crowd using hands as well as lips. Most tools that isolate a target speaker lean on lip motion synced to the speech. But people also gesture as they talk, and those gestures line up with stressed words and beats.

Adding gesture cues gives the system a second clock to lock onto. That should help when lips are hidden, blurred, or turned away from the camera. Cleaner single voice tracks serve hearing aids, meeting tools, and any setting where many people talk at once.
arxiv-2601-19030:
Philip Amortila, Audrey Huang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, and Nan Jiang unify a key idea in judging policies from logged data. Off-policy evaluation asks how well a new rule would do, using data logged under an old one. In the linear case, error bounds hinge on a coverage number that says how well the old data covers the new rule's path.

Many past bounds each define coverage in their own way. The team gives one view that ties them together. A single lens on coverage helps researchers compare results and spot which assumptions truly drive the error in such studies.
arxiv-2601-19230:
Dimitrios M. Thilikos and Sebastian Wiederrecht study what happens when a graph is banned from containing a whole surface's pattern. The great Graph Minors Structure Theorem covers graphs that avoid a fixed minor. Such a graph splits into pieces that almost lie on a surface. That surface is one where the banned graph cannot sit.

Their work refines that picture by excluding surfaces themselves as minors. Structure theorems of this kind are the backbone of graph theory: they turn a ban into a blueprint. Algorithms often ride on such blueprints, since a graph with known structure is far easier to search and color.
arxiv-2601-19530:
Ettore Budassi and eight colleagues refine a measurement tool used at electron-positron colliders. The tool is called radiative return. Instead of scanning many beam energies, physicists run at one energy and use radiated photons to sample lower ones. The target is the pion form factor, a function that describes how pions respond to electric charge.

That function feeds into a key calculation: the hadronic part of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Small errors there matter, since the muon value is a sharp test of known physics. The authors bring the radiative return method to a high accuracy standard that mixes fixed-order results with resummation. Sharper inputs mean a cleaner verdict on whether the muon hides new physics.
arxiv-2601-19630:
Matías G. Delgadino and Scott A. Smith study a classic model from statistical physics. The O(N) linear sigma model describes fields with N components and a symmetry between them. They place the model on a two-dimensional plane and scale it following the large N expansion. In that limit, many quantities become computable.

The authors show that correlations in the model decay exponentially fast. The model also acquires a mass, a gap that controls how far influences reach. That mass itself decays exponentially as the temperature parameter varies. Proving mass generation in such models is a long-standing goal in mathematical physics. The result adds a rigorous case to a field built on formal arguments.
arxiv-2601-19730:
Hongxu Chen, Ke Wei, Xiaoming Yuan, and Luo Luo study how machine learning models train under messy noise. In practice the random noise in gradient estimates has heavy tails, meaning extreme values occur often. That picture fits real training better than the usual bounded-noise assumption. Most theory under heavy tails covers how fast training converges.

Far less is known about generalisation: how well the trained model does on new data. The authors analyse stability and generalisation bounds for nonconvex optimization with heavy-tailed noise. Nonconvex problems are the norm in deep learning. Bounds like these explain when training will transfer to unseen examples. The work closes a gap between optimisation theory and learning practice.
arxiv-2601-20130:
Haoxuan Wang and five colleagues work on making robots act in real time. A robot that pauses to think can react too late, since the world keeps moving while it plans. Recent systems use asynchronous inference: the next chunk of actions is predicted while the current chunk still runs.

The authors present a method based on masked action chunking for this setting. The aim is smooth control with no gaps between what the robot does now and what it plans next. Fast, steady action matters for robots that handle objects or move through changing spaces, where even small delays can spoil performance.
arxiv-2601-20230:
Haoyuan Yu, Yuxuan Chen, and Minjie Cai present a framework for full-duplex voice dialogue, where a system listens and speaks at the same time. Natural conversation needs this overlap; turn-taking systems feel slow by contrast. The authors break dialogue into minimal conversational units, so each unit can be processed on its own.

Their system predicts when to move from one unit to the next. It is built around a multimodal large language model, with voice activity detection and speech synthesis as supporting parts. The setup works without task training, in a plug-and-play manner. Smoother voice dialogue would help assistants feel more like talking with a person.
arxiv-2601-20330:
Zhuang Chen and six colleagues present PsychePass, a way to judge how well large language models do therapeutic work. Models show promise in mental health care, but judging their skill is hard because counseling is unstructured and unfolds over long sessions. The authors say current evaluation has an unanchored defect.

That defect shows up as process drift, where a simulated client wanders off the counseling goal, and standard drift, where fixed scoring stays unstable. PsychePass anchors evaluation in trajectories and compares models in tournaments. Steadier measures matter before any model is trusted near real patients.
arxiv-2601-20630:
Wen-Tao Lyu and Eulogio Oset propose a reaction to search for a predicted exotic particle. It is a pentaquark-like state with strangeness, near a mass the authors give in energy units. The state is expected at lower mass than comparisons with known pentaquark states would suggest. The authors argue that coupled channels play an important role in setting that mass.

They propose a specific decay of the lambda-b baryon into a phi meson, an eta-c meson, and a lambda baryon. Giving experimenters a concrete channel to measure is how predicted states get found, or ruled out.
arxiv-2601-18530:
Aliasghar Sarizadeh studies how a set of maps acts when it is run again and again on a tight space. Each map in the set is a two-way move that keeps the shape of the space whole. Run as a group, the maps build a kind of cloud of forms. A twin set, built from the back moves, runs the cloud in reverse.

The work asks when the group act stays smooth as the start point shifts a bit. It also asks how keen that act is to small shifts in the maps them-selves. Smooth acts are a base for the maths of fractals, where clouds of forms grow from plain maps. Keen acts can break a fractal with a breath. Proofs here help sort which map sets give calm clouds and which give wild ones.
arxiv-2601-18630:
Abeer Badawi and eight colleagues grade how well language models help with health of the mind. More people seek help than there are trained staff to give it. That gap makes smart chat tools a tempting path to help at scale. A chat tool can be warm and quick, yet warmth is not the same as good care. Its words must be safe, apt, and in line with what trained staff would prize.

The team grade chats on more than one trait at once, with human judges. Traits can pull in unlike ways: a warm reply may still be unsafe. A score per trait shows where a tool is strong and where it is frail. Such grades could help clinics pick tools with care. They could also set a bar that tools must clear before they meet the public.
arxiv-2601-18730:
Henry Bell and five colleagues build a way to teach language models a set of writ rules in the open, with the chain of thought on show. In the main path, rules are taught by score-based training that hides why a reply counts as good. Staff who must trust the tool can't see which rule drove a call. That gap counts when the rules touch fair play and harm.

Their tool, named Reflect, has the model state the rule it uses as it works. The chain can then be read, checked, and fixed by staff. A tool that shows its rules could be held to them in a real way. It could also serve at scale, since the check is part of the run, not a next step. The work aims at trust by sight, not by faith.
arxiv-2601-21330:
Avijit Mandal and Henry D. Pfister extend a quantum message-passing method for reading signals sent as quantum states. The method offers a cheaper option than measuring all signals jointly. Until now, its design and analysis covered only binary alphabets, where each signal is one of two states.

The authors generalize it to alphabets with many symbols. They focus on symmetric channels whose output structure has a tidy circular form. That form lets the analysis tools carry over to the larger alphabet. Cheaper decoding for richer alphabets matters for future quantum links, where each signal should carry more than a single bit.
arxiv-2601-21530:
S. Simón-Díaz reviews how large spectroscopic surveys have reshaped the study of massive stars. These surveys gather spectra, the fingerprints of starlight, for huge numbers of heavy stars. Spectra reveal a star's heat, makeup, spin, and motion.

The review lays out the main surveys and what their data have shown. Several familiar readings of the signals turn out to be far more tangled than once thought. Massive stars drive the life cycle of galaxies, forging elements and ending as supernovae. Sharper readings of their spectra feed better models of how they live and die.
arxiv-2601-21630:
Metha Prathaban, Charlie Hoy, and Michael J. Williams speed up the analysis of gravitational wave signals. Full Bayesian analysis of a wave event is rigorous but very costly. Fast methods exist, yet their results are rarely used to guide the full analysis.

The authors present a way to reuse the fast estimates inside the final inference. Their repartitioning keeps the prior independent of the data, so the statistics stay rigorous. That balance gives speed without cooking the books. Faster final answers matter when telescopes must chase a fading source within hours of a detection.
arxiv-2601-22430:
Rudrajit Choudhuri, Christopher Sanchez, Margaret Burnett, and Anita Sarma ask what daily AI use does to how students think. Their 2026 preprint notes that many students now use generative AI in coursework. Past work looked at one-off help-seeking; this work asks about habit-level shifts.

The team study whether routine use ties to weaker cognitive engagement, the deep work of thought itself. The stakes are high: habits formed in school can last for years. Clear evidence can guide teachers, not just ban or bless the tools. The work frames the right questions. It seeks facts over fear.
arxiv-2601-22530:
Tung Sum Thomas Kwok and five co-authors train table-question agents with rewards for each checkable step. TableQA asks a model to answer from a table, but the answer needs a chain of changes to the table state. Their 2026 preprint notes that this chain, not a static read, is the hard part.

Rewards tied to each table change give the agent true feedback as it works. That should cut wild leaps that land on a lucky answer. It should also yield a trace a human can audit. The work aims at agents that do data chores with proof. Each step can be checked.
arxiv-2601-21930:
G. Théret, D. Sugny, and C. Latune compare ways of counting entropy production in small quantum systems. Entropy production measures how irreversible a process is. For two-level systems open to an environment, the literature offers several definitions, born from different settings and motives, and they do not always agree.

The authors set those definitions side by side and analyze how each relates to memory effects, where the environment feeds information back into the system. They use a concrete example: a qubit coupled to a single bosonic mode acting as a finite environment. Their 2026 preprint helps physicists choose the right entropy measure for quantum thermodynamics experiments, where sloppy definitions can flip conclusions.
arxiv-2601-22030:
Chengyi Cai and co-authors refine a popular trick for making language models forget private information. Task arithmetic unlearns by computing a task vector, the change in parameters caused by tuning on the private data, and subtracting it from the model. The method is fast and simple.

Its flaw is over-forgetting: one blanket subtraction can damage parameters that other knowledge depends on. The team's 2026 preprint proposes per-parameter task arithmetic, scaling the subtraction parameter by parameter. Surgical forgetting matters because privacy requests, from personal data to copyrighted text, increasingly require removal that does not lobotomize the model. Finer control could make unlearning a routine operation rather than an emergency procedure.
arxiv-2601-22130:
Lakshya Gupta and co-authors build a proving ground for language model agents inside enterprise software. Frontier models excel as autonomous agents in many domains. They remain untested, though, in complex business systems where hidden workflows trigger cascading effects across interconnected databases.

Their 2026 preprint introduces World of Workflows, a benchmark that brings world models to enterprise systems. An agent must predict how an action in one system ripples into others, much as an employee learns that one form updates five records. Enterprise automation is where agent failures get expensive and quiet, so a benchmark that exposes hidden dependencies could prevent costly surprises in deployment.
arxiv-2601-22230:
Peijia Qin and co-authors improve the judges that pick the best generated code. Test-time scaling for code generation often samples many candidate solutions and lets a language model judge select the best. Training a reliable judge is hard because the candidates shift in distribution, with severe imbalances between good and bad samples.

Their 2026 preprint presents DaJ, a data-reweighted language model judge for test-time scaling in code generation. Reweighting the training data counters those imbalances, so the judge learns to spot the faults that actually appear at test time. A better judge multiplies the value of every extra sample, making test-time scaling cheaper for coding assistants.
arxiv-2601-20830:
Waldyn Martinez builds a detector for odd points in messy process data. The 2026 paper presents VSCOUT, a hybrid method based on a variational autoencoder. Modern plants and services produce data that defy classic control charts. The data are high-dimensional, skewed, and prone to contamination. Heavy tails and multiple modes break the assumptions of classical statistical process control.

The setting is retrospective monitoring: looking back over past data. Rare special-cause points can warp the baseline itself. That warp can mask true anomalies and hide them in plain sight. VSCOUT aims to find a clean in-control reference set despite the mess. A sound reference set is the base for all later alarms. The method serves industries that must spot real faults in noisy records.
arxiv-2601-20930:
Emilie Burnham and a large team model how galaxies built their stars over time. Their 2026 paper gives a forward model for star formation histories. It targets galaxy groups seen in the early universe. JWST shows such galaxies with a wide range of brightness and color. The question is whether their star formation ran smooth or in bursts. The title warns the answer is more complex than it looks.

A forward model starts from a proposed history and predicts what telescopes would see. Matching those predictions to data tests the history. Bursty growth leaves traces that steady growth does not. The model infers the recent history of whole groups, not single galaxies. That shapes how we read the JWST census. It helps decide if early galaxies were calm builders or flickering ones.
arxiv-2512-01230:
Howard Wiseman analyzes the entropy carried by a laser beam in a 2025 physics paper. A laser beam is often modeled as a pure coherent state, the cleanest quantum state of light. In fact its state is mixed, even when its photon counts follow the statistics of a coherent state, because its phase must wander over time.

Wiseman considers an ideal laser beam whose phase diffuses at a rate equal to its spectral width. He works out the entropy flow of such a beam, the rate at which it carries entropy away. The result corrects a common idealization and matters for quantum optics and precision measurement.
arxiv-2601-23030:
Gefan Yang, Frank van der Meulen, and Stefan Sommer infer hidden processes that evolve along trees. Observations may exist only at the leaves, as with species traits at the tips of an evolutionary tree. Exact smoothing for nonlinear dynamics is intractable, and particle methods weaken in high dimensions.

Their neural framework, NBFFG, guides sampling forward using a backward filtering pass learned by a network. It handles both jump transitions and smooth diffusions in one scheme. Better tree inference helps biology, epidemiology, and other fields with branching data. Sparse, leaf-only observations define the difficulty: everything between the root and the tips must be inferred, not seen.
arxiv-2601-23230:
Adrien Cogez and seven co-authors assess whether the space observatory LISA can detect gravitational-wave memory. Memory is a permanent deformation of spacetime left behind after a wave passes. It is a direct prediction of general relativity that has never been observed.

LISA, a future laser interferometer in space, may record signals strong enough to show the effect. Their Bayesian approach weighs how confidently memory could be claimed from noisy data. A detection would confirm a subtle, lasting fingerprint of gravity itself. A Bayesian treatment suits the question, since detection claims for memory must weigh signal evidence against instrument noise.
arxiv-2512-00330:
Quantum dots and point contacts show sharp peaks in conductance that can signal the Kondo effect, a many-body phenomenon. Jongbae Hong classifies such coherent peaks in two-terminal quantum devices in 2025. The classification splits peaks into normal and anomalous Kondo peaks.

The split rests on the underlying spin dynamics and on the scaling function that the temperature-dependent conductance collapses onto. Sorting peaks correctly matters because similar-looking curves can hide different physics. Device physicists can use the scheme to read experimental conductance data with more confidence about which mechanism is at work. Two-terminal devices are the simplest testbeds, which makes the classification cleaner to state. Scaling collapse is a strong test, because unrelated curves rarely fall on one function.
arxiv-2512-03130:
Odd red galaxies seen by the Webb telescope puzzle astronomers. Kohei Inayoshi and Luis Ho review what these objects, called Little Red Dots, might be in this 2025 work. Deep surveys found them in large numbers, and they are classed as active galactic nuclei.

Their traits do not fit the standard picture of feeding black holes. Many ideas have been put forward for how such black holes form and grow so early. The authors weigh the options in a critical review. The answer could reshape views of the first massive black holes. For black hole scholars, the review sorts bold claims from what the data truly show.
arxiv-2512-03230:
Galaxy motions can reveal how fast structures grow. R. J. Turner and a large team measure that growth in this 2025 work. They use data from the DESI first data release peculiar velocity survey.

The team studies correlation functions, which show how galaxy positions and motions link across space. They work with both the galaxy field and the momentum field. Growth rate measures test whether gravity matches Einstein's theory on large scales. They also help pin down the nature of dark energy. Correlation methods use many galaxy pairs, which beats noise down as samples grow.
arxiv-2512-03530:
Mixed states can still hide protected edge features. Yoshihito Kuno studies edge bits in average symmetry protected topological states in this 2025 work. The state is guarded by one strong and one weak symmetry of the same kind.

Like pure protected states, these mixed states possess edge bits. The author shows an analogous operator response exists, tied to symmetry fractionalization. Edge bits in mixed states matter because real quantum systems are never perfectly pure. The work extends topological ideas toward realistic, noisy conditions. Operator responses give an experimental handle, since edge bits alone are hard to see.
arxiv-2512-01730:
Ángel Castro and Daniel Lear study how swirling flows behave in a flat, two-dimensional fluid, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their subject is the linearized Euler equations, which describe small disturbances around a round vortex whose strength falls off steadily with radius. Earlier work showed that such steady fall-off makes disturbances fade and settle into rings.

Castro and Lear show the picture is more delicate than it seemed. They build nearby vortex profiles that no longer fall off strictly, only weakly, and for these profiles they find non-round solutions that repeat in time instead of fading away. The result marks a sharp edge case: change the profile just slightly, and the calming effect of damping can disappear.
arxiv-2512-01930:
Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient, or SVRG, is a training method that corrects noisy gradient steps with occasional exact ones to speed up learning. Nico Daheim and three co-authors show in 2025 that this older method has surprising, deep connections to a recent Bayesian technique called posterior correction.

SVRG and its variants promised faster training yet never caught on widely in deep learning. Viewing the method through the Bayesian lens explains its behavior in a new way and suggests fresh variants. The connection also gives posterior correction, developed for a different purpose, an unexpected second life as a tool for understanding optimization.
arxiv-2512-02030:
Glioblastoma is the most aggressive form of brain tumor, and new treatments are urgently needed. Hao Qian and seven co-authors describe a 2025 framework that designs therapeutic peptides, short protein chains, aimed at a potential target protein called ATP5A, then tests the designs in the laboratory.

Their pipeline runs dry to wet: generative models propose peptides first, and experiments validate them afterward. A lead-conditioned generative model focuses the search near known lead peptides, in regions of the right geometry. That focus tames the combinatorial explosion of designing from scratch. The work shows generative design and bench testing closing the loop on a hard cancer target.
arxiv-2512-02130:
Classifying whole graphs, molecules, social networks, or biological structures, demands features that capture both neighborhood detail and global shape. Ahmet Sami Korkmaz, Selim Coskunuzer, and Md Joshem Uddin present a 2025 representation learning method that watches topology from more than one view at once.

Graph neural networks excel at local structural patterns but often overlook global topological features that decide a graph's identity. Adding a topology-aware cross-view corrects that blind spot, combining the two kinds of evidence. Stronger graph representations feed directly into drug screening, network analysis, and bioinformatics, where shape at every scale carries meaning.
arxiv-2512-02230:
Office work in finance runs through a tangle of digital tools, and routine processes still suffer human error and delay. Rory Milsom's 2025 dissertation study builds a finance-focused simulation of that environment and tests whether a general-purpose language model agent can complete wealth-management tasks accurately and economically.

The study extends an existing agent benchmark, TheAgentCompany, with representative wealth-management workflows. An agent that could handle such tasks reliably would change how back offices staff routine work. The results speak to both accuracy and cost, the two measures firms actually weigh before trusting software with client business.
arxiv-2512-02330:
Some metals turn superconducting in ways no one can yet fully explain. Their electrons both roam and sit still in fixed spots. M. A. Zeb gives a new idea in 2025. The crystal field near the still electrons shakes. That shaking can pull the roaming ones into pairs.

The same small hops that make the Kondo effect also shake the field. Zeb builds the pairing force out of that shake. The force is not the same in all directions, so it favors some pair shapes over others. A fresh pairing idea counts, since new superconductors are found by guessing right about the glue.
arxiv-2512-02830:
Mohamed Awad, Mahmoud Mohamed, and Walid Gomaa ask whether defending a vision model also sharpens its attacks. Deep networks excel at image tasks but break under small crafted perturbations, called adversarial examples. Adversarial training, which practices on such attacks, is the leading defense for robustness.

The team studies a side effect few have checked: attack transferability. If robust models craft examples that fool other models more easily, defense quietly upgrades offense. Knowing this trade off helps security teams weigh the true cost of hardening models that will be shared or sold. A shield that forges swords is not a pure loss, but it is a fact a buyer has a right to know up front.
arxiv-2512-03030:
Elba Alonso-Monsalve examines how to build a Hilbert space for gauge theories when the gauge group is infinitely large. Physical states need an inner product, a rule for measuring overlaps. With infinite volume gauge groups, states do not inherit that rule in any straightforward way.

Different quantization procedures then give prescriptions that may not agree. Group averaging is one route through the problem. Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, a solvable two dimensional theory, serves as the test bed. Settling these foundations matters for any quantum theory of gravity, however simple the model. Toy worlds earn their keep when the rules they teach still hold in the big one. This toy is built to teach rules of just that kind.
plos-pone-0010030:
The authors were Olga Gil, Ivan Díaz, Cristina Vilaplana, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a tuberculosis model in minipigs. A low dose of the TB bacterium was given through the chest. The pigs were then watched for twenty weeks as infection took hold.

Immune readings showed a strong Th1 type response and a weak antibody response. Tissue checks showed how granulomas, tight balls of immune cells, formed around the germs. The title names the key point: walling germs inside granulomas helps contain TB in this model. The model gives TB researchers another animal system to study.
plos-pone-0010130:
The authors were Reyhan Nergiz-Unal, Judith Cosemans, Marion Feijge, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at blood clots on ruptured artery plaques. When plaque breaks, platelets build a clot, and a signal called ADP helps stabilize it. That signal works through receptors named P2Y12 on platelets.

Most earlier models damaged healthy vessels, which may not match real heart attacks. Studying clots on ruptured plaques under flow, the team confirmed a stabilizing role for P2Y12. The result supports drugs that block that receptor to prevent dangerous clots. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010230:
The authors were Lawrence Bish, Kevin Morine, Meg Sleeper, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked what a muscle growth brake does in the heart. Myostatin is well known for holding back skeletal muscle growth. Its role in heart muscle, though, was controversial, with studies pointing in different directions about benefit and harm.

The team studied heart cells under stress, in culture and in a mouse model. Stress raised myostatin through a route that depends on the Erk signal. The raised myostatin then held back heart cell growth, naming a control loop worth watching in heart disease.
plos-pone-0010330:
Arnaud Bertrand, Michael Ballón and Alexis Chaigneau used sound to map life in the ocean for PLOS ONE in 2010. Deep water in some regions holds very little oxygen. These low-oxygen zones are growing as the climate warms and human effects add up. Most sea animals cannot live far down into such water. Their depth limit, though, is hard to watch directly.

Echo sounders, which bounce sound off animals below, offered a way. The reflections showed where living things stopped as depth increased. That stopping line marked the top edge of the low-oxygen zone. Tracking that edge over time could reveal how fast the zones expand. For fish and the people who depend on them, the stakes are direct.
plos-pone-0009830:
Some HIV drugs work by blocking the virus from fusing with human cells. Pedro Matos and colleagues studied two such fusion inhibitor peptides, enfuvirtide and T-1249. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The team watched how the peptides interact with cell membranes. They used membranes from erythrocytes, red blood cells, and lymphocytes, white blood cells of the immune system. How a drug peptide meets the membrane affects how well it can work. Membrane contact is the first step in blocking fusion. The details help chemists design stronger fusion blockers.
